Grammar Notes
1. -ba form <conditional form of verbs and adjectives>
Both verbs and adjectives can take the -ba conditional form (also called the provisional form), meaning "if..."
The rules for forming the -ba form of verbs are as follows:
Group I (godan) verbs:
Change the final u-dan kana of the verb to the corresponding e-dan kana, then add "ば". For example:
Group II (ichidan) verbs:
Change the final kana "る" of the verb to "れ", then add "ば". For example:
Group III (irregular) verbs:
① Suru-verbs: change the final "る" to "れ", then add "ば". That is:
② Kuru-verb: change the final "る" to "れ", then add "ば". That is:
来る：くる→くれ＋ば＝来れば
① ネットで調べれば、必要な情報は何でも手に入ります。／If you look it up online,
you can get any information you need.
② 軽い風邪は、ゆっくり休めば治りますよ。／A slight cold will get better if you rest well.
③ 今すぐ電車で行けば、まだ間に合いますよ。／If you go by train right now,
you'll still make it in time.
The rules for forming the -ba form of adjectives are as follows:
I-adjectives: change the final "い" to "ければ".
※ Note: when the i-adjective "いい" takes "ば", first change "いい" to "よい",
giving "よければ".
Na-adjectives: attach "ならば" to the stem; in modern Japanese the "ば" is usually omitted, leaving just "な
④ 安ければ買いたいけど、安くなければ買わない。／If it's cheap I want to buy it;
if it's not cheap, I won't buy it.
⑤ 作り方が簡単なら、私も作る。／If the recipe is simple, I'll make it too.
When the negative form of a verb (V ない) is made conditional, it follows the adjective conjugation rule, that is:
⑥ 今すぐ行かなければ、間に合わない。／If we don't go right now,
we won't make it.
2. 〜たり〜たりする <alternation; listing: たり-1>
Replace the "た" of the verb ta-form / i-adjective ta-form with "たり", and attach "だったり" to na-adjectives/
nouns, forming "〜たり〜たりする". It expresses several actions or states alternating within the same period,
or an action or state occurring repeatedly. Two words of opposite meaning can also take "たり"
to show an action repeating back and forth (as in example ②).
たり、見学したりしていたんですか。／Nakamura, when you were in England, did you always go around
with the group, visiting places together?
They played, opening and closing the door over and over.
ます。／These days it's been raining and blowing hard — cold every day.
④ 部活は月曜日だったり、水曜日だったりして、決まっていません。
／Club activities are sometimes on Monday, sometimes on Wednesday — it's not fixed.
"〜たり〜たりする" can also be used to give examples, picking out two or three representative cases
from several things or actions. In modern Japanese it is more common to list just one example, so it often
appears as "〜たりする". It can be translated as "...and things like that" or "...or something".
The conjugation is the same as the grammar above.
① 道に迷ったりしなかったんですか。／Didn't you get lost or anything?
たりしていましたよね。／When there was no internet, we used to travel with a copy of
"How to Walk the Earth" in hand.
③ 昨日は資料を届けに外出したりしていたので、ほとんど席にいま
せんでした。／Yesterday I was out delivering documents and such, so I was hardly at my desk.
4. V てある <resulting state of an object>
A transitive verb followed by "てある" mainly expresses that after someone has deliberately done something,
the resulting state continues to exist. It can be translated as "(something) has been ...-ed (and remains so)".
With "V てある", the verb is usually a volitional transitive verb, and its object is marked with "が" instead.
a. 壁にポスターが貼ってあります。／There is a poster (put up) on the wall.
b. ポスターを壁に貼りました。／(Someone) put the poster up on the wall.
Compared with sentence b, sentence a emphasizes the state in which the poster remains on the wall
after having been put up.
① A：この辞書、だれのですか。／Whose dictionary is this?
／I think it's Kobayashi's. There's a name written on the cover.
② この件について課 長にはすでに報告してあります。／Regarding this matter,
I have already reported it to the section chief.
／Come to think of it, that travel guide is sitting on my bookshelf at home too.
Pattern: V る + ように、〜
The dictionary form or nai-form of a verb followed by "ように" forms a purpose clause, expressing that one does
(or doesn't do) something so that a certain state comes about; it can be translated as "so that...".
The main clause that follows generally expresses the means or action taken to achieve that purpose.
Note that the verb before "ように" is usually a non-volitional verb such as "なる" or "できる",
or a weakly volitional form such as the potential or negative form.
社します。／So that I can have dinner with my family, I always leave work at 6 p.m.
② 後ろの席の人にも見えるように、字を大きくしました。／So that people in the back seats
can see too, I wrote the characters bigger.
③ 明日寝坊しないように、今夜早く寝ましょう。／So that we don't oversleep tomorrow,
let's go to bed early tonight.
を手に持って旅行していました。／In the days before the internet, so as not to get lost,
people traveled with "How to Walk the Earth" in hand.
6. 〜そうだ <appearance>
Pattern: V ます stem + そうだ.
An adjective stem or the masu-stem of a verb followed by "そうだ" expresses the speaker's conjecture
based on appearance or past experience. Equivalent to "looks like..." or "seems..." in English.
① あの人はいつも寂しそうです。／That person always looks lonely.
② このテーマなら、すぐに論文が書けそうですね。／With this topic,
it looks like the paper could be written right away.
③ このテーブルは足が太くて、丈夫そうです。／This table has thick legs;
it looks sturdy.
"そうだ" can also modify a noun in the form "〜そうな", or modify a verb/adjective
in the form "〜そうに". For example:
④ あの子は大事そうに人形 を引き出しにしまった。／The child carefully put the doll away in the drawer, as if it were precious.
It introduced the history of travel destinations, local food, and even listed
番号も載せたりしていて、役に立ちそうな 情報がたくさん書いて
ありました。／It also had inn phone numbers printed — full of useful-looking information.
Also, the adjectives "いい" and "ない" take "そうだ" in the forms "よさ
そうだ" and "なさそうだ" respectively. For example:
⑥ どうかしましたか。あまり元気がなさそうですね。／Is something wrong?
You don't look very well.
⑦ この子は体が丈 夫そうではない。／この子は体が丈夫ではなさ
そうだ。／This child doesn't look very strong.
The masu-stem of a verb followed by "切る" forms a compound verb expressing the thorough completion
of the action (as in examples ①②), or that an action or state has reached its limit (as in examples ③④).
／That long novel was so interesting I finished it in a week.
ません。／Her cooking is delicious, but I can't finish it all by myself.
③ 最近毎日残業 しているので、疲れ切っています。／I've been doing overtime every day lately,
so I'm completely exhausted.
／Why must one spell out something so obvious?
Expression Notes
"そういえば" is used when something comes to mind mid-conversation, or to change the topic.
It is often used to bring up a shared topic one has just recalled or something one has experienced.
It can be translated as "come to think of it..." or "now that you mention it...".
／Come to think of it, you said you wanted to climb Mt. Fuji sometime.
② A：そういえば、知ってる？／Hey, come to think of it, did you know?
B：なに？／What?

1. V るべきだ <should; ought to>
The dictionary form of a verb followed by "べきだ" expresses that one must or should do something; translate as "should/must ...".
Its negative form is "べきではない", meaning it is better not to do so; "should not ...".
When "する" takes "べきだ", it can be either "するべきだ" or "すべきだ".
① お年寄りに対して、あんな言葉遣いで話すべきではない。／You shouldn't speak to elderly people
with language like that.
② お年寄りに対して、あんな言い方をするべきではない。／You shouldn't talk to elderly people
in that manner.
③ 大学時代はいろいろな体験をすべきだと思う。／I think you should experience many things
during your university years.
④ 学生は学校のルールを守るべきです。／Students should follow the school rules.
"V るべきだ" can also modify a following noun; when it does, use the form "V るべきN", for example:
⑤ どこか直すべきところはありますか。／Is there anywhere that should be fixed?
⑥ 彼女に言うべきことを全部言った。／I said everything I ought to say to her.
Pattern: V attributive form ＋わりに（は）
A attributive form ＋わりに（は）
The attributive form of a verb or adjective, or "N＋の", followed by "わりに（は）" expresses that the result
in the latter clause does not match what would naturally be expected from the former. Translate as "...yet...", "for..."
① 人生経験が豊かなわりには、人を見る目がない。／For all his rich life experience,
he has no eye for people.
った。／I didn't study much, yet I did pretty well on the last exam.
③ 昨日の講演会は、思ったわりには人が集まらなかった。／Yesterday's lecture
drew fewer people than expected.
④ 海に近いから、気温が高いわりには、暑く感じないね。／Being near the sea,
it doesn't feel hot for how high the temperature is.
Pattern: plain sentence ＋からには、〜
A plain-style sentence (nouns and na-adjectives drop "だ" and take "である") followed by "からには"
expresses the speaker's judgment based on the situation in the first clause; the latter clause often uses
expressions of conjecture, suggestion, determination, wish, or obligation. Translate as "since...; now that...".
① 代表になって全国大会に出るからには、優勝を目指したい。／Now that I'm going to the national tournament
as a representative, I want to aim for the championship.
Since you're living in Japan, you'd better be able to speak some Japanese.
③ 生きているからには、楽しく生きよう。／Since we're alive, let's live happily.
The nai-form of a verb followed by "で" is the negative continuative form: doing the latter action
without doing the former, or the latter happening instead. Translate as "without ...-ing".
Don't lower the evaluation bar; replace them with questions that are easier to answer.
② もう疲れたから、観光に行かないで、直接ホテルに帰ろう。／I'm tired already, so let's skip sightseeing
and go straight back to the hotel.
③ 子供が来ないで、親が来た。／The child didn't come; the parents came instead.
④ お風呂に入らないで寝てしまった。／I went to sleep without taking a bath.
Pattern: A / A / V plain form ＋なら
We learned earlier that a noun followed by "なら" highlights a topic (Lesson 15). Besides nouns,
plain-style sentences can also take "なら" to form a conditional, used to state one's own opinion or judgment
based on what the other person said or the situation at hand. The latter clause of "なら" often uses
expressions of judgment, volition, command, request, or evaluation. Translate as "if..., (then) ...".
① 買い物に行くなら、 醤油も買ってきてもらえる？／If you're going shopping,
could you buy me some soy sauce?
If that was the case, you should have told me earlier.
③ 親まで反対しているなら、その夢は 諦 めたほうがいいよ。／If even your parents
are against it, you'd better give up that dream.
A noun followed by "に加えて" expresses that something else is added on top of that thing or event,
or another event occurs in addition. Mostly used in written language. Translate as "in addition to...; plus...".
① 激しい雨に加えて、強い風も吹いている。／Heavy rain, plus strong wind blowing.
② 日本語に加えて、英語も上手だ。／On top of Japanese, she's good at English too.
／This area has not only rich natural scenery but also many historical buildings.
Pattern: V ます stem ＋やすい
The masu-stem of a verb followed by "やすい" or "にくい" forms a derived adjective meaning the action
is easy or hard to do. For example:
There is neither a convenience store nor a supermarket nearby, so it's very inconvenient to live here.
Enlarging the phone's font makes it easier to read.
／Our senior is smart; he can explain anything very clearly.
8. 〜おかげだ。<cause of a positive result>・〜せいだ。<cause of a negative result>
Pattern: V attributive form ＋おかげだ（・せいだ）.
A / A attributive form ＋おかげだ（・せいだ）.
The attributive form of a verb/adjective, or "noun+の", followed by "おかげだ" expresses the cause of
a positive result. It often appears as "〜おかげで、〜", with the latter clause describing how the speaker
concretely benefited. Translate as "thanks to...".
Thanks to everyone's help, the presentation went smoothly.
In contrast to "〜おかげだ", the attributive form or "noun+の" followed by "せいだ" expresses the cause of
a negative result. It can also appear as "〜せいで、〜" or "〜せいじゃない", meaning "it's all ...'s fault",
"just because of...", or "it's not ...'s fault".
③ 今回の失敗は、すべてわたしのせいです。／This failure is entirely my fault.
Because of your delays, the project wasn't finished before March.

1. V（よ）う <volitional form of verbs>
The volitional form of a verb expresses the speaker's will, a suggestion, etc. Its conjugation rules are as follows:
Change the final u-dan kana of the verb to the corresponding o-dan kana and add "う". For example:
Drop the final kana "る" of the verb and add "よう". For example:
辞める：やめる＋よう＝辞めよう
寝る：ねる＋よう＝寝よう
(1) Suru-verbs: change "する" to "し" and add "よう". That is:
(2) Kuru-verb: change "来る" to "来" and add "よう". That is:
来る：くる→こ＋よう＝来よう
"V（よ）う" is the plain form of "Vましょう". It can express the speaker's own intention to do
the action, as in example ①; or that the speaker and listener do the action together, usually translated
as "let's ...", as in example ②. In Japanese, this pattern of doing something together is also often
used to suggest that the listener do something — a rather indirect, soft way of suggesting, as in example ③.
① Polite: 私も（本を）借りてきましょう。／I'll go borrow one too.
Plain: 私も（本を）借りてこよう。
② Polite: いっしょに映画を見に行きましょう。／Let's go see a movie together.
Plain: いっしょに映画を見に行こう。
③ Polite: 道を渡る時、横断歩道を使いましょう。／When crossing the road, use the crosswalk.
Plain: 道を渡る時、横断歩道を使おう。
The volitional form followed by "と思う" gives "V（よ）うと思う", mostly used in the first person
to express the speaker's intention to do something — "I'm determined to..." / "I think I'll...". Unlike (what we learned in Lesson 19)
Compared with "V るつもりだ" (intend to do...) learned earlier, "V（よ）うと思う" uses the
volitional form "V（よ）う", so it more strongly reflects the speaker's
will and inner drive toward taking that action.
① 日本のアニメが大好きで、日本語を学ぼうと思いました。／I love
Japanese anime so much that I decided to learn Japanese.
I wanted to exercise, so I bought running shoes.
③ 今夜は久しぶりに映画を見ようと思います。／Tonight I think I'll watch a movie
for the first time in a while.
3. 〜たら、〜た。 <discovery>
Pattern: V た + ら
We learned earlier that verbs, nouns, and adjectives followed by "たら" form a conditional. When the main
clause ends in the past tense — the "〜たら、〜た" pattern — it expresses that when the event before "たら"
occurred, the result in the latter clause turned out differently from what was expected. The latter clause is often
something beyond the speaker's control, a new discovery, or a surprise.
① 昼は暑かったのに、夜になったら、とても寒かった。／It was hot at noon,
but when evening came, it turned (surprisingly) cold.
② 買い物に行ったら、店は閉まっていた。／I went shopping, only to find the store
was closed.
③ 家に帰ったら、誰もいなかった。／When I got home, (I found) nobody was there.
4. 〜のに。 <dissatisfaction>
We learned the adversative "のに" used mid-sentence. "のに" can also come at the end of a sentence,
expressing regret or dissatisfaction that the actual result differs from what was expected from the preceding clause.
It generally need not be translated.
① 必ず来ると約束してくれたのに。／He promised me he would definitely come. (and yet...)
② あと一分早ければ、終電に間に合ったのに。／If I'd been just one minute earlier,
I would have made the last train.
③ え？売り切れた？買いたかったのに。／Huh? Sold out? I really wanted to buy it.
The particle "って" is the colloquial form of the quotation particle "と". Sometimes it can be used alone
with the following verb omitted, as in example ②.
① 今日は学校に行きたくないって言っていますよ。／(He) says he doesn't
want to go to school today.
② 母:お父さん何だって？／What did your dad say?
いって。／He said the flight was canceled, so he probably can't come back tonight.
③ メールしてねって言ったのに。／He told me to email him. (and yet...)
A verb followed by "V てしまう" expresses the speaker's regret, remorse, or dismay that the action happened.
In colloquial speech, "V てしまう" also becomes "V ちゃう".
I lost it, and now I'm in trouble.
② いつもかぎを忘れてしまう。／I always end up forgetting my keys.
③ 言ってはいけないことを言っちゃった。どうしよう。／I said something I shouldn't have.
What should I do...
Pattern: N＋の＋ため（に）、〜
A/A /V attributive form + ため（に）、〜
"Noun + の" or the attributive form of a verb/adjective followed by "ため（に）" describes a cause.
When "ため（に）" describes a cause, the result is often unfavorable, and the tone is formal, mostly written.
① 台風が近づいているため、今日の学校は休みになりました。／Because a typhoon

③ 今日の会議は出席者が少なかったため、早く終わった。／Today's meeting

To attach "ずに" to a verb, use the continuative of the negative form: drop the "ない" of the nai-form;
for the Group III verb "する", it becomes "せず" before "ず".
"V ずに" is the written form of "Vないで" and modifies the following clause adverbially:
doing the latter action without (doing) the former.

Pattern: plain sentence / noun だ ＋といっても、〜
A noun or the plain form of a verb/adjective followed by "といっても" forms a concessive clause. The main

／There's a park near the hotel. Though calling it a park, it's really just a small courtyard.

expensive, it's not so expensive that you can't pay it.
／Although I lived in Africa, it was actually only three months.

becoming part of it. Note that a noun or na-adjective stem can directly take the question particle "か".

3. V るようになる <change>
The dictionary form of a verb followed by "ようになる" expresses change: gaining an ability (from being unable
to do something to being able to do it), or acquiring a habit (from not doing something to doing it). For example:
① 積極的に自分から意見が言えるようになった。／(I've become) able to
express my own opinions proactively.
② 隣 の子供は最近きちんとあいさつするようになった。／The neighbor's kid
has started greeting people properly lately.
③ 日本語が話せるようになりました。／I've become able to speak Japanese.
4. 〜し、〜 <listing; coordination>
Pattern: plain sentence + し、〜
The particle "し" attaches to a clause: two or more "し"-clauses can be coordinated to list reasons;
or a single "し"-clause can cite just one reason among several.
Translate as "both...and...", "what's more...".
It's raining, and the wind is strong too — let's cancel our date.
② このアパートは静かだし、日当たりもいいし、とても快適だ。／This apartment
is quiet, and it gets good sunlight — very comfortable.
ましょう。／I got my bonus today, so let's go eat something nice at a fancy restaurant.
"〜に対する・〜に対して" usually attaches to nouns referring to people or abstract things, indicating
the target of an action, feeling, or attitude — "toward(s)...; regarding...". "〜に対する" can modify a noun;
to modify a predicate, use the form "〜に対して + predicate".
① 林 さんに対する尊敬心はいつごろからのものですか。／Since when have you
looked up to Mr. Lin?
② マスコミに対して、「ノーコメント」を繰り返した。／To the media, he repeatedly
said "no comment".
③ この学校の先生たちは、学生に対して本当にやさしいです。／The teachers at this school
are truly kind to their students.
With a purpose or reason as premise, the conditional "V ば" followed by the adjective "いい" can be used
to give advice or state a suitable method or means — "you can...; ...will do; just..."
① その仕事が嫌なら、やめればいい。／If you don't like the job, just quit.
② この町の歴史なら、山田さんに聞けばいいですよ。／If it's about this town's history,
you can ask Yamada.
③ A：頭が痛い…／My head hurts...
B：この薬を飲めばいいよ。すぐ治るよ。／Take this medicine. You'll get better
right away.
The te-form of a verb followed by "てみる" expresses trying something out — "try ...-ing".
② 留学 のことはもう一度親と相談してみます。／About studying abroad, I'll try discussing it once more

③ わからないことは、あの人に聞いてみればいいです。／If there's something you don't understand,
try asking that person.
Pattern: N の + ために
"Noun + の" or the dictionary form of a verb followed by "ために" expresses purpose. When "ために"
expresses purpose, the subjects of the two clauses must be the same, and the action in the main clause
should be a volitional verb aimed at achieving that purpose.
To learn about Japan's traditional culture, I studied the tea ceremony.
② 転職のために、いろいろ面接を受けた。／To change jobs, I went to various interviews.
③ 家を買うために、朝から晩まで働く。／To buy a house, I work from morning to night.
Pattern: V る／V ている／V た＋ところ、〜
"ところ" follows the plain verb form, "V ている", or "V た", highlighting the point in time within the
course of the action — with the nuance that the main clause's event interrupts the ongoing state of the subordinate
clause. Similar to the "V る／Vている／Vた＋ところだ" learned in Lesson 24, "V るところ" marks a point just
before the action happens, "V ているところ" a point while it is in progress, and "V たところ" a point just
after it has happened. Depending on the verb in the main clause, particles such as "に、を、へ、で"
can follow "V る／V ている／V た＋ところ".
てきた。／Just as the drama I'd been looking forward to was starting, a phone call came in.
It was just about to end when, at that very moment, it was called off due to rain.
③ ようやく工事が始まったところ（に）、台風が来た。／Construction had finally just begun,
when the typhoon came.
Pattern: V ます stem ＋そうにもない
Lesson 26 covered "〜そうだ" for appearance. The negative form of the masu-stem + "そうだ" is
"〜そうにもない"; the "に" and "も" can each be omitted, giving "〜そうにない" or "〜そうもない".

no way I'll pass.
③ この問題は 難 しすぎて、僕にはわかりそうもない。／This problem is too hard;
there's no way I can understand it.

1. 〜と、〜 <condition>
Pattern: N だ + と、〜
The dictionary form of a verb or i-adjective, or "noun/na-adjective + だ", followed by "と" forms a
conditional sentence expressing that whenever the former holds, the latter invariably follows.
Translate as "when... (then)...", "if..., ...". This pattern is also often used when giving directions, as in ④.
① スイッチを入れると、部屋が明るくなります。／When you flip the switch, the room
lights up.
② 貧乏だと、就 職も結婚もできない。／If you're poor, you can neither find a job
nor get married.
③ 気温が低いと、桜が咲きません。／If the temperature is low, the cherry blossoms won't bloom.
④ まっすぐ行くと、左 手に大きな駐車場が見えます。／Go straight, and on your left
you'll see a large parking lot.
The te-form of a verb followed by "ておく" expresses doing something in advance for a certain need,
or keeping a certain state as a temporary measure — "...in advance; ...and leave it (as is)". In speech,
"V ておく" often contracts to "V とく".
Before leaving, please charge the car in advance.

3. 〜ことになる <outcome; arrangement>
Pattern: V る＋ことになる
The dictionary or nai-form of a verb followed by "ことになる" expresses a result arising from the natural
course of events; the form "V る／V ない＋ことになっている" expresses an established rule or arrangement, e.g.:
① 2年後には帰国することになると思います。／I think I'll end up returning home in two years.
② 来年の4月に日本に 留学することになりました。／It's been decided that I'll go study in Japan
in April next year.
③ 工場見学に行く人は、20日までに申請のメールを出すことになって
います。／Those going on the factory tour are required to send the application email by the 20th.
We learned that the particle "まで" follows a time or place to mark a range. "まで" can also follow
nouns other than time/place to express extent, often with the speaker's surprise — "even...; to the point of...".
① 由加ちゃんまで花粉 症になった。／Even Yuka has come down with hay fever.
② 内定をもらったし、彼女もできた。さらに、宝くじまで当たった！／
I got a job offer and a girlfriend. And on top of that, I even won the lottery!
③ 近頃、子供だけでなく、大人まで漫画を読んでいる。／These days, not only children
but even adults read manga.
Pattern: N な + のに
V/A attributive form + のに
"Noun + な" or the attributive form of a verb/adjective followed by the particle "のに" forms an adversative
compound sentence: the premise or cause in the first clause does not lead to the expected result in the second.
The speaker often sounds surprised or dissatisfied. Translate as "...yet...; although...". Both clauses of "のに"
are usually established facts; in particular, the second clause cannot be a command, request, or wish.
① まだ4月なのに、夏よりも暑い。／It's only April, yet it's hotter than summer.
② 今日は大雪が降っているのに、朝から授業がある。／It's snowing heavily today, yet
we have classes from the morning.
③ もう薬を飲んでいるのに、体調はぜんぜん良くならない。／I'm already taking medicine,
yet I'm not getting any better.
6. 〜らしい <hearsay>
"らしい" attaches to the plain form of a verb/adjective (na-adjectives drop だ) or a noun, expressing hearsay
or conjecture based on objective grounds — "it seems...; I hear...; apparently...". The objective source can be
marked with "〜によると" or "聞いたところでは".
① 聞いた 話 では、田中さんは来月仕事を辞めるらしいです。／From what I hear,
Tanaka is apparently quitting his job next month.
② 会長は今日欠席するらしいですよ。さっき連絡が入りました。／It seems the chairman
will be absent today. A notice just came in.
③ あの人は業界ではかなり有名らしい。／That person seems quite famous in the industry.
A noun followed by "だらけ" expresses that something is all over a place, in a derogatory sense —
"covered with...; full of...; riddled with...".
① 子供たちは泥だらけになって、遊んでいる。／The children are playing, covered in mud.
② 母：ほら、部屋中 はほこりだらけだよ。掃除しましょうよ。／Look,
the room is covered in dust. Let's clean up.
It's already full of scratches, but because it's so precious to me, I can't bring myself to throw it away.
Pattern: N の + 途中（に／で）、〜
An action noun + の, or the dictionary form of a verb, followed by "途中（に／で）" expresses that before
the action is completed, something else happens; or that something exists on the way somewhere —
"on the way...; midway through...". The particle "に／で" after "〜途中" can be omitted.
① 会社に行く途中で、急に気分が悪くなって倒れた。／On the way to work,
he suddenly felt sick and collapsed.
② 通学の途中 に、たくさんくしゃみが聞こえた。／On the way to school, I heard
lots of sneezing.
③ 大学に行く途中、高校時代の友達に会った。／On the way to university, I ran into
a friend from high school.
Pattern: N の + ような気がする
V/A attributive form + ような気がする
"Noun + の" or an attributive form followed by "ような気がする" is similar to the conjecture "ようだ"
learned earlier. "〜ような" modifies the following noun "気". "気がする" means "to have a feeling",
"to feel somehow". Here "気" can be replaced by "感じ" or "予感".
"〜ような気がする" is often paired with adverbs like "なんとなく" and "何だか".
It corresponds to "I feel like...; I have a feeling that...".
① 何だかもう仕方がないような気がします。／I somehow feel there's nothing more to be done.
② 運動のあと、なんとなく 体 が軽くなったような感じがする。／After exercising,
I somehow feel my body has become lighter.
③ あの人にはどこかで会ったような気がします。／I have a feeling I've met
that person somewhere before.
10. V た/V ないほうがいい <advice>
The ta-form or nai-form of a verb followed by "ほうがいい" expresses advice or recommendation —
"you'd better (do)...; it would be better not to...".
① わからないときは、先生に聞いたほうがいいと思います。／When you don't understand,
I think you'd better ask the teacher.
② 体が弱いんだから、無理をしないほうがいいですよ。／You're weak, so you'd better
not push yourself.

1. 〜につれて <as; along with>
Pattern: V る＋につれて
After a noun expressing change (action, phenomenon, etc.) or the dictionary form of a verb, "につれて"
expresses that as the former situation changes or develops, the latter changes or develops accordingly.
Both clauses of "につれて" should be verbs or nouns expressing change. Translate as "as...; along with..."
① 期末テストが近づくにつれて、どんどん不安になる。／As the final exams
draw nearer, I get more and more anxious.
② 大人になるにつれて、好みも変わっていく。／As you become an adult, your tastes
change too.
③ 経済の発展につれて、海外旅行する人も多くなりました。／As the economy
developed, more people started traveling abroad.
2. V ていく/くる <movement; change>
The te-form of a verb followed by "ていく" or "てくる" indicates the direction of movement or change.
I. Movement
"ていく" and "てくる" can follow a movement verb to show the direction of the action, or a stative verb
to show moving while maintaining that state. "V ていく" and "V てくる" can be translated as "...and go"
and "...and come" respectively. "V てくる" can also mean doing something and then coming
back, as in example ③.
① 病院へ行く途中で、お見舞いの花を買っていきましょう。／On the way to the hospital,
let's buy some flowers for our visit.
② この川は富士山から流れてくる。／This river flows down from Mt. Fuji.
③ ちょっと待って。本を持ってくるね。／Hang on. I'll go get the book.
II. Change
A. "V ていく" presents a prospect from now into the future, or the continuation of a developing process
or state — "...on; keep ...-ing; go on ...-ing" (may be left untranslated).
① この事件は継続的に 調査していく必要があります。／This case needs to
be investigated continuously going forward.
② これからもがんばっていきましょう。／Let's keep doing our best
from now on.
B. "V てくる" presents a gradual change from the past or continuation of a state; the form "V てきた"
can also express the strengthening of a feeling or emotion, as in example ① — "...has come to...; ...has started to...".
／It's past 12 and my daughter still isn't home. I can't help starting to worry.
② 寒くなって、風邪をひく人が多くなってきた。／It's gotten cold, and more people
have started catching colds.
3. 〜そうだ <hearsay; quotation>
A plain sentence followed by "そうだ" expresses hearsay or reported information. The hearsay expressed by
"〜そうだ" cannot be the speaker's own direct inference; it is indirectly heard or reported. The source
can be made explicit with "〜によると", "〜によれば", "〜では", etc.
① 担当者の 話 によれば、新発売の 商品は 1日で売り切れたそうです。
／According to the person in charge, the newly released product sold out in one day.
② 今回の試験の合格率は 5％だったそうだ。／I hear the pass rate for this exam was
③ 予報では、台風は今夜 上陸するそうだ。／According to the forecast, the typhoon will make landfall tonight.
A plain sentence followed by "ということだ" sums up, paraphrases, or explains the facts stated before.
Such an explanation is mostly the speaker's inference, judgment, or evaluation.
① えっ？山田さんはまだ来ていませんか。つまり、また遅刻したという
ことですね。／Huh? Yamada still isn't here? So that means he's late again.
５万円にもならないということだ。／800 yen an hour — in other words, even working
Monday to Friday, you wouldn't make 150,000 yen a month.
いけないということです。／Japanese restaurants have gone completely non-smoking. In other words,
you may not smoke inside the establishment.
"にかけて" follows a noun of time or place to express a range, usually in the form "〜から〜にかけて"
— "from ... to ...". Similar to "〜から〜まで", but "〜から〜にかけて" has no clear boundary,
loosely spanning two points in time or space.
① 今月から来月にかけて仕事を休むつもりです。／I plan to take off from this month
through next month.
② 今夜から明日の早朝 にかけて大雨だそうです。／They say there will be heavy rain from tonight
through early tomorrow morning.
③ 東京から京都にかけてかなり暑くなるでしょう。／It will get pretty hot
from Tokyo to Kyoto.
A noun or dictionary-form verb followed by "ごとに" expresses each recurrence of a repeated event,
or every single complete occurrence — "every...; each...".
① この目覚まし時計は５分ごとに鳴る。／This alarm clock rings every 5 minutes.
② 国ごとにそれぞれの文化や 習慣がある。／Every country has its own culture
and customs.
③ 感染予防のために、１時間ごとにエレベーターを消毒する。／To prevent infection,
the elevators are disinfected every hour.
A noun followed by "によって" expresses a basis or grounds for judgment, often used with words
like "違う" — "depending on...; it varies with/by...".
① 人によって、考え方が違う。／Ways of thinking differ from person to person.
② 時によって、やり方を変えたほうがやりやすいかもしれない。／Depending on the occasion,
changing the approach may make it easier to do.
③ 私 はその日の気分によって、服を変えます。／I change my clothes depending on my mood
that day.
A noun followed by "として" expresses the capacity or status in which the subject acts — "as..."
① 今年の 4月から、弁護士として働くことになった。／Starting this April,
I will work as a lawyer.
② 彼女は女優として活躍している。／She is active as an actress.
As a husband and as a father, I will always cherish this family.
The dictionary or nai-form of a verb followed by "ようにする" expresses making an effort to do (or not do)
something so as to reach a goal or state. Often paired with adverbs like "できるだけ" and "なるべく" —
"to make a point of...; to try to...".
① 最近太ったから、毎日５キロ走るようにしています。／I've gained weight lately, so I make a point of
running 5 kilometers every day.
② 高校時代は自分から意見を言わないようにしていた。／In high school, I made a point of
not voicing my own opinions.
③ 約束を守るようにしてほしい。／I want you to keep your promises.
④ 甘いものは食べないようにしている。／I make a point of not eating sweets.
Pattern: V る＋ことだ
The dictionary or nai-form of a verb followed by "ことだ" indirectly offers advice or a gentle instruction
to the listener. Mostly used in everyday conversation.
① 痩せたいなら、毎日運動することだ。／If you want to lose weight, you should exercise every day.
If you want good grades, you mustn't slack off on your studies.
③ A：友達を増やしたいけど、どうすればいいですか。／I want to make more friends —
what should I do?
B：サークルに入って違う学部の人と話してみることですよ。／You should join a club
and try talking to people from other departments.

Pattern: V te-form + て、〜
The te-form of a verb or i-adjective followed by "て", or a noun or na-adjective stem followed by "で",
forms a clause expressing a mild cause. The main clause can only state objective facts — not commands,
suggestions, or other volitional expressions. When the negative of a verb takes "て" for a reason,
use the form "V なくて" (as in example ③).
① 工場の近くは汚染がひどくて、変な臭いがする。／The pollution near the factory is terrible,
and there's a strange smell.
② 字が下手で、恥ずかしいです。／My handwriting is bad, so I'm embarrassed.
③ 昨日は夜遅くまで仕事が終わらなくて、大変でした。／Yesterday I couldn't finish work until late at night;
it was rough.
④ 久しぶりに友達に会えて、とても嬉しいです。／I'm so happy I could see a friend
after a long time.
2. 〜たら、〜 <condition>
Pattern: V ta-form + たら、〜
"たら" can attach to verbs, nouns, and adjectives, forming a hypothetical conditional —
"if/when... (then)...". In use, the content before "たら" is assumed to have come true, and the latter
clause (main clause) expresses the speaker's inference about the possible result, or a request to the listener.
The latter clause of "〜たら、〜" can also express the speaker's will, instructions, commands, or suggestions.
① わからないことがあったら、何でも聞いて。／If there's anything you don't understand,
ask me anything.
② 仕事がきつかったら、すぐに辞めてしまう若者は多くいる。／Many young people
quit right away if the job is tough.
If it's a girl, I want to name her "Yuko".
④ 田中さんが来たら、会議を始めましょう。／When Tanaka arrives, let's start the meeting.
3. 〜か <choice>
Verbs, adjectives, and nouns can all take "か" to select among or list the options before it —
① 夏休みはシンガポールかタイに行きたい。／For summer vacation I want to go to Singapore or Thailand.
② 晩ご飯はお寿司かラーメン、どっちがいい？／For dinner, sushi or ramen —
which is better?
③ バスで行くか、地下鉄で行くか決めよう。／Let's decide whether to go by bus
or by subway.
④ 留学に行くか、就 職 するか、かなり悩んでいる。／Whether to study abroad or get a job —
I'm really torn.
Pattern: V/A attributive form + 場合（は）、〜
The attributive form of a verb/adjective, or "noun + の", followed by "場合（は）" picks out one situation
from among the possibilities and states the measure to take or judgment to make should it occur —
"in the case of...; if/when...".
① 来週の休みが1 日の場合は市内で、2日間ある場合は郊外でセミナー
をしましょう。／If next week's break is one day, let's hold the seminar in the city; if it's two days,
in the suburbs.
② 地震が起きた場合は、まず火を消さなければなりません。／If an earthquake occurs,
you must first put out the fire.
If stairs are inconvenient, please use this elevator.
④ 熱が続く場合は、病 院に行ったほうがいい。／If the fever persists, you'd better go to the hospital.

The dictionary or nai-form of a verb followed by "ことにする" expresses a personal decision to do something.
① もう眠いから、明日早く起きて宿題をすることにします。／I'm too sleepy,
so I've decided to get up early tomorrow and do my homework.
② 今日からお酒を飲まないことにする！／As of today, I'm giving up alcohol!
③ この冬休みはこれまで学んだ知識を復習することにしました。／This winter vacation
I've decided to review what I've learned so far.
The dictionary form of a verb followed by "ことはない" expresses the speaker's view that there is no need

or "わざわざ〜ことはない".
／This exam is just easy questions, so there's no need to worry at all.
／You can book online, so there's no need to go out of your way to call.
ないと思う。／Smartphone apps are so convenient that I don't think you need to bother with a paper map.
Pattern: plain sentence ＋のではないか（と思う）
A plain sentence (for nouns and na-adjectives in the non-past, the final "だ" changes to "な") followed by
"のじゃないか" expresses an uncertain conjecture — "might...?; I wonder if...; perhaps...".

We learned to use the te-form of verbs for sequential continuation, as in sentence a. This form is mostly
colloquial; in written Japanese or formal settings, the masu-stem of the verb can also express sequential
continuation, as in sentence b.

combine with the negative form (V ない); when the masu-stem is a single syllable (e.g. "来", "見", "出"),

3. Prohibitive form
Opposite to the imperative, Japanese verbs also have a prohibitive form meaning "do not do..."
It is formed by adding "な" to the dictionary form. Likewise, prohibitive commands are mostly
masculine speech, or used in orders, sports cheering, warnings, and notice boards.
① 危険！近づくな。／Danger! Keep away.
② 秘密だから、絶対に人に言うなよ。／It's a secret — absolutely don't tell anyone.
③ 関係ないことを聞くな。／Don't ask about things that don't concern you.
The plain form of a verb or adjective (mainly i-adjectives and dictionary forms) followed by "くらい"
cites a concrete case to illustrate the degree of the thing or state just described. "くらい" can
be replaced by "ほど".
① そんなの困るよ。泣きたいくらいだよ。／That's so troublesome. I could cry.
② 歩けないくらい膝が痛い。／My knees hurt so much I can't walk.

10. 〜と思われる <spontaneous form of verbs>
In Japanese, the "V（ら）れる" form can express that an emotion arises naturally (自然に発生する);
this usage is called 動詞の自発 — the "spontaneous" use of verbs. The spontaneous form is identical
in shape to the passive form.
Not every verb has a spontaneous use. Common verbs that can express spontaneity in the -（ら）れる form
include mental-activity verbs such as 案じる→案じられる, 思い出す→思い出される, 思う→思われる,
考える→考えられる, 感じる→感じられる, 偲ぶ→偲ばれる. With the spontaneous form, the experiencer
is usually the speaker, made explicit with "私は" or "私には", or omitted.
Thinking and feeling are mental activities; this lesson's "思われる" expresses that a thought or feeling
comes to mind naturally; its content is quoted with "と". For example:

1. Honorific language and special honorific verbs
The Japanese honorific system is vast and complex, involving many parts of speech such as verbs, nouns, and adjectives. As for honorific
verbs, they can be divided into two types according to the subject: honorific language (尊敬語) and humble language (謙遜語).
A. Honorific language (respectful)
Honorific language is a way of expressing respect toward the agent of the action mentioned in the conversation. When using honorific
language, the subject should be the respected party.
Honorific verbs that express respect include:
行く・来る＝いらっしゃる/おいでになる
Among these, the verbs “いらっしゃる”, “おっしゃる”, “なさる”, and “くださる”
become “いらっしゃいます”, “おっしゃいます”, “なさい” respectively when followed by ます.
When using special honorific verbs, simply replace the predicate verb in the sentence with the corresponding
honorific verb.
① 先生も講演会に来ますか。／Will you also come to the lecture, Sensei?
→先生も講演会にいらっしゃいますか。
② お名前は何と言いますか。／What is your name?
③ 大学でどんな研究をしていますか。／What kind of research are you doing at
university?
→大学でどんな研究をなさっていますか。
④ 資料を見てください。／Please look at the materials.
B. Humble language
Humble language is an expression by which the speaker shows respect to the listener or the respected person indirectly, by using humble words.
When using humble words or humble language, the subject should be the speaker themselves or a member of
their own group.
Verbs that express humility include:
行く・来る＝参る
会う＝お目にかかる
Among these, the verb “存ずる” becomes “存じます” when followed by ます. When using special humble
verbs, simply replace the predicate verb with the corresponding humble verb.
⑥ 営業事業部に配属が決まり、とても嬉しく思います。／I am very happy to be as-
signed to the Sales Business Division.
→営業事業部に配属が決まり、大変嬉しく存じます。
／Tomorrow I will visit your lab, Sensei. Thank you in advance for your guidance.
2. お/ご〜する <humble>
In addition to the special honorific verbs above, humility can also be expressed with the pattern
“お/ご〜する” to achieve a polite effect. The specific rules for this pattern are as follows:
お + masu-stem of a native (wago) verb
ご + stem of a Sino-Japanese (kango) verb
Note: this pattern cannot be used when removing ます from the masu-form leaves only a single mora
① では、挨拶を願います。／Then, please give a greeting (to everyone).
② 新 しく営業事業 部に配属することになったインターン生を 紹介
します。／Let me introduce the intern newly assigned to the Sales Business Division.
→ 新 しく営業事業部に配属することになったインターン生をご
③ 先生、荷物を持ちましょうか。／Sensei, shall I carry your luggage?
The masu-stem of a verb followed by “つつ” indicates that the action in the first clause and the action described in the second clause occur simultaneously;
similar in meaning to “ながら”, but with a stiffer tone, mostly used in written language or more formal situations.
ります。／While improving our existing models, our company is also trying to develop new products.

考えています。／I would like to move the project plan forward while discussing it with everyone.
“〜にわたって” or “〜に” follows nouns indicating period, place, range, or number of times,
and “〜にわたる” is used to express spanning the entire range.

An action noun or the dictionary form of a verb followed by “に伴い” indicates that, accompanying the action or change in the first
clause, a corresponding change occurs in the second clause. Mostly used in written language; can be translated as “as ..., ...”.
It can also be written as “〜に伴って”.

As children grow, they begin to show interest in all kinds of things.

Pattern: V/A/A/N attributive form + わけだ
The attributive form of a verb or adjective followed by “わけだ” is used to state a fact: based on certain
causes or reasons in the preceding context, the speaker infers that the first clause is the inevitable result of how that fact developed. It can express both that the
speaker inevitably draws such a conclusion from established facts, trends, or reasoning, and that the speaker subjectively accepts
this cause-and-effect relationship.
かりしているわけだ。／I heard Sato stayed up all night writing a manuscript. No wonder he's been
yawning since morning.
ぎが違った。／He struggled desperately to open the door, but it wouldn't open. Of course it wouldn't — the key was
wrong.

graduation, many students wear black suits.

がったわけです。／Because night owls are increasing, that's why there are so many convenience stores.
The dictionary form or ない-form of a verb followed by “よう（に）” expresses a wish or hope for oneself or
others. The polite form of the verb can also be used before “よう（に）”; after “よう（に）” it is often paired with verbs like “願う”,
“祈る”, and “祈願する”, and is used in written language or more formal situations.
① いい人に出会えるよう、神様に祈った。／I prayed to God that I could meet a good person.
② みなさまのお力になれるよう、頑張ります。／I will do my best, hoping
to be of help to everyone.
Pattern: V る + に従って
A noun (mostly a suru-verb stem) or the dictionary form of a verb followed by “に従って” indicates that as
the change in the first clause progresses, the second clause changes accordingly. Can be translated as “as ...”.
① 年をとるに 従 って、白髪やシワが増えてきた。／As I get older,
gray hairs and wrinkles have increased.
② 使いこなせる単語の数が増えるに従って、日本語の進歩を実感でき
るようになりました。／As the number of words I can use skillfully increased, I began to really
feel my Japanese improving.
／As the economy developed, people began to use things up and throw them away.
“向け” after a noun means “aimed at ...” or “suitable for ...”. The noun before “向け”
is usually a certain group of people or organization. “N向け” can be followed by a noun in the form “N向けの” (as in
example ①), or modify a predicate in the form “N向けに” (as in example ②).

A plain-form sentence followed by “とは限らない” indicates that things are not necessarily as stated in the first clause, often implying
that exceptions exist. Can be translated as “not necessarily ...” or “not always ...”.
いよ。／Even if you wait in a long line, that shop's ramen is not necessarily good.
② 天気予報はいつも当たるとは限りません。／Weather forecasts are not always accurate.
／It's not necessarily not on the exam, so let's review this part as well.
Pattern: N さえ + V/Aば
V (suru-verb stem) + さえ + すれば
“さえ〜ば” forms a conditional clause expressing that as long as the condition described in the first clause holds, the conclusion or
result in the second clause will be realized. Can be translated as “as long as ..., ...”.
ある。／As long as it's a design I like, I sometimes buy it without looking at the price.
少なくない。／Quite a few parents think that as long as their children study, they don't have to
do anything else.
／Cup noodles can be eaten as long as there is hot water — very convenient.
The te-form of a verb followed by “てはいられない” expresses that, in an urgent situation, one can no longer continue the state or

He was really too inept; I couldn't just watch without helping.

14. 次第
Pattern: V ます + 次第
The masu-stem of a verb followed by “次第” expresses temporal sequence: as soon as the first clause is realized, the action
of the second clause is performed immediately. This pattern mainly conveys the speaker's volition to do the second action.
① 信号が変わり次第、発車いたします。／As soon as the signal changes, we will depart.
② スケジュールが決まり次第、ご連絡いたします。／Once the schedule is decided, we will imme-
diately contact you.
③ 準備が整い次第、向かいます。／As soon as preparations are complete, we will set out.
④ 新しい情報が入り次第、改めてお伝えします。／As soon as new information comes in,
we will let you know again right away.
A noun followed by “の下で” or “の下に” indicates acting under the influence or control of that person or
thing. Can be translated as “under ...”.
① 先生の温かいご指導の下で、博士論文を書き上げた。／Under my teacher's warm
guidance, I completed my doctoral dissertation.

2. Japanese passive sentences I: direct passive sentences <basic passive sentences A, B>
In Japanese, a sentence whose subject is the agent of the action is called an “active sentence”, and one whose subject is the receiver of the
action is called a “passive sentence” (Japanese: 受け身文). The correspondence between Japanese “active sentences” and “passive sentences”
is as follows:
a. 先生が学生をほめました。<active>／The teacher praised the student.
b. 学生が先生にほめられました。<passive>／The student was praised by the teacher.
a. 上司は私に仕事を頼みました。<active>／The boss assigned me work.
b. 私は上司に仕事を頼まれました。<passive>／I was assigned work
by the boss.
In example (1-a), “先生” is the agent of the action “ほめる (to praise)”, while the
receiver of the action is “学生”, marked with the particle “を” in the active sentence. When converted to the passive sentence (1-b), the
receiver “学生” becomes the subject, marked with “は” or “が”; the agent
“先生” must be marked with the particle “に”, and the verb “ほめる” changes to its passive form “ほ
められる”. This pattern can be summarized as:
Direct passive sentence A: N が/は N に/から V（ら）れる
Here, N is the receiver of the action, marked with “が/は”; N is the agent, marked with “に/
から”. In basic passive sentences, both the receiver N and the agent N should be people.
In example (2-a), “上司” is the agent of the action “頼む”, while the receiver is
“私”, but the direct object of the predicate verb “頼む” is “仕事”. Therefore, in the passive sentence (2-b),
the direct object “仕事” of the predicate verb still needs to be marked with “を”; the receiver “私”
becomes the subject of the passive sentence, marked with “は” or “が”; the agent “上司” can
be marked with the particle “に” or “から”; the verb “頼む” changes to its passive form “頼まれる”.
This pattern can be summarized as:
Direct passive sentence B: N が/は N に/から N を V（ら）れる
Here, N is the receiver of the action, marked with “が/は”; N is the agent, marked with “に/か
ら”; N is the direct object of the action, marked with “を”. As with direct passive A, in direct pas-
sive B, both the receiver N and the agent N should be people.
Among the many types of Japanese passive sentences, the “direct passive” is semantically neutral, and its “active”
and “passive” versions can mostly be interchanged. For example:
① お母さんは子供を起こしました。／The mother woke the child up.
→子供はお母さんに起こされました。／The child was woken up by the mother.
② 日本政府は、高橋さんを招待した。／The Japanese government invited Takahashi.
→高橋さんは日本政府に 招待されました。／Takahashi was invited by the Japanese government.

The possessor passive is mainly used to describe that something belonging to the receiver of the action, or a part of their body, is affected by some ac-

Possessor passive: N が/は N に N を V（ら）れる

4. Japanese passive sentences III: indirect passive sentences
The “indirect passive” refers to cases where the action does not directly affect the subject (mostly first person), but
the subject suffers or is troubled by some event or someone else's action — an indirect effect; some books also call it the “adversative
passive”. Since predicate verbs can be divided into intransitive and transitive verbs, the “indirect passive” has the following
two patterns:
Indirect passive (intransitive verb): N が/は N に V（ら）れる
Indirect passive (transitive verb): N が/は N に N を V（ら）れる
Here, N is the adversely affected party, serving as subject marked with “が/は”; N is the actor, marked with the particle “に”.
The indirect passive expresses that N suffers an adverse ef-
fect or damage due to some unintentional action of N. When N's action is a transitive verb, its object N is marked with “を”.

5. Japanese passive sentences IV: non-emotive passive sentences
The Japanese “non-emotive passive” is closest in usage to the English passive. This is mainly due to the influence of the mass
translation and introduction of European and American literary works starting in the Meiji period, which gradually
popularized the use of the “non-emotive passive”.
The “non-emotive passive” is often used to state well-known social phenomena, with a thing or matter as the subject.
Depending on whether the agent of the action needs to be explicitly stated, the “non-emotive passive” can be divided into two types:
Non-emotive passive A (unspecified agent): N が/は（N に）V（ら）れる
Whether or not the agent (the doer of the action) is a specific person, the key fea-
ture of the “non-emotive passive” is that the subject N must be a “thing or matter”, marked with “が” or “は”. The agent is marked with “に”,
and since the agent is not a specific person, “N に” is generally omitted.
① この教会は600年前に建てられました。／This church was built 600 years ago.
② 日本語は多くの人に学ばれています。／Japanese is studied by many people.
③ 地震で、多くの家屋が壊されました。／Many houses were destroyed in the earthquake.
Non-emotive passive B (specified agent): N が/は N によって V（ら）れる
The “non-emotive passive B” is mainly used to describe inventions, creations, or new discoveries. In this case the
agent (doer of the action) N must be explicitly stated and marked with “によって”.

by Natsume Soseki.
⑥ 『スズメの戸締り』は新海誠監督によって作られました。／Suzume was cre-
ated by director Shinkai Makoto.
A plain-form sentence, or the stem of a na-adjective or a noun followed by “かどうか”, is used to present the two possibilities,
affirmative or negative. Equivalent to “whether or not ...”.

A noun followed by “らしい” forms a derived adjective expressing that something has the typical characteristics of what the noun denotes.

The causative form of Japanese verbs is formed by attaching “せる” or “させる” to the verb stem. The specific conjuga-
Change the final u-row kana of the verb to the corresponding a-row kana and attach “せる”.
Note: verbs ending in “う” first change to “わ” before attaching “せる”. For example:
Type II verbs: remove the final kana “る” of the verb and attach “させる”. For example:
(1) Suru-verbs: change “する” to “させる”. That is:
(2) Kuru-verb: change “来る” to “来”, then attach “させる”. That is:
来る：来る→来＋させる＝来させる
2. Japanese causative sentences I: transitive causative sentences
Causative sentences express making someone do something, allowing someone to do something, etc.; they can be translated as “let/make ... (some-
one) do ... (something)”. According to the transitive/intransitive distinction, Japanese causative sentences fall into “transitive causative
sentences” and “intransitive causative sentences”. The basic pattern of a “transitive causative sentence” is:
Transitive causative sentence: N は/が N に N を V（さ）せる
N is the causer, serving as subject marked with “は” or “が”; N is the causee (the doer of the action),
marked with the particle “に”; N is the direct object of the action, marked with “を”. For example:
① a. 店員が本を並べます。／The shop assistant arranges the books.
b. 本屋の主人が店員に本を並べさせます。／The bookstore owner has the shop assistant arrange the
books.
Example ①a is an active sentence: the doer of the action, “店員”, is the subject, and “並べる” is the action of the subject.
In contrast, example ①b is its causative sentence: here “本屋の主人” becomes the subject who makes the assistant arrange the
books, while the doer “店員” becomes the causee in the “transitive causative sentence”,
marked with “に”; the direct object of the action “並べる” is “本”, marked with “を”. It is worth
noting that Japanese causative sentences are mostly used for a superior causing a subordinate to act. When a subordinate asks a superior to do something,
the causative form is generally not used.
② 母親は息子に食器を洗わせました。／The mother had her son wash the dishes.
す。／In kindergarten, the teacher has the children draw pictures and write kanji.
④ お母さんは美紀に早く彼氏を作らせようとしている。／The mother is trying to get Mi-
ki to find a boyfriend soon.
3. Japanese causative sentences II: intransitive causative sentences
Intransitive causative sentences express making someone do something, allowing someone to do something, or causing someone to feel a cer-
tain emotion, etc.; they can be translated as “let/make ... (someone) ... (do something)”. When the causative verb in a Japanese causative sentence is in-
transitive, the doer of the action can be marked with “を” or “に”. The basic pattern is:
Intransitive causative sentence: N は/が N に/を V（さ）せる
N is the causer, serving as subject marked with “は” or “が”; N is the causee, and also
the doer of the action, marked with “を” or “に”. It is worth noting here that, when the doer's will
is disregarded and coercion is expressed, “を” is usually used (as in example ①); when the doer's will
is considered and permission is implied, the doer can be marked with “に” (as in example ②).
① コーチはもう走れないという選手を無理やり走らせた。／The coach forced a player

The te-form of a verb followed by “てはじめて” describes that only after the experience or event of the first clause

A/A attributive form + まま
“Verb + た”, “noun + の”, or the attributive form of an adjective followed by “まま” describes keeping the state of the first clause

loquial.

2. Causative-passive sentences
Simply put, the causative-passive sentence is closer to an active sentence. For example:
① a. 私は漫画を捨てた。<active>
b. 私は漫画を捨てさせられた。<causative-passive>
In the examples above, the doer of the action in both a and b is “私”, and the action is the same: throwing away the manga.
Using the causative-passive form of the verb highlights the doer's psychological unwillingness and
displeasure when performing the action. The basic pattern of the causative-passive sentence is:
Here, N is the doer of the action, serving as subject marked with “は” or “が”; N is the
causer, i.e. the person or organization that makes N do something, usually marked with “に”; when emphasis on a
specific causer is needed, “から” or “によって” can also be used. But in causative-passive sentences, the causer
is generally omitted — example ①b omits it; N is the direct object of the action — in example ①b,
“漫画の本” is the direct object of the action “捨てる”, marked with “を”.
② 子供のころは、嫌いなものでも親に食べさせられました。／When I was a child,
my parents made me eat things even if I didn't like them.
③ この子には心配させられることが多い。冒険が好きな子なのだ。／This
child makes me worry a lot. He's a child who loves adventure.
④ この仕事は初めてなのに、一人で全部やらされました。／Although this job was
my first time, I was made to do it all by myself.
The plain form of a verb or adjective followed by “ものだから” is used to state a reason. The pat-

clause after “ものだから” cannot express the speaker's will, commands, etc. When “ものだから” appears mid-sentence, the
form “もので” can also be used.

The te-form of a verb followed by “てからでないと” indicates that something is no good unless the first clause is completed first —

Pattern: V た + あげく
The ta-form of a verb, or an action “noun + の”, followed by “あげく”, indicates that after going through the process
described in the first clause, the result described in the second clause is finally reached. The first clause often implies repeated attempts,
a long time spent, or great effort, while the second clause is mostly a regrettable result. Can be translated as “...,
and in the end ...”, “after ..., ended up ...”.
“あげく” can also be used with the following predicate in the forms “あげくに” or “あげくの果てに”.
It can also modify a following noun in the form “あげくの”.
They often quarreled and finally broke up.

parents endless worry over money and friends, he finally left home.

dicates performing the action of the second clause, or describing its state, within the period indicated by the first clause. Can be translated as “while

Pattern: V/A/A attributive form + 上（に）
The attributive form of a declinable word, or “noun + の/である”, followed by “上（に）”, indicates that, on top of the existing

The ta-form of a verb followed by “たらどうですか” is used to suggest that the listener do something. When the two speakers are close,

morrow?

Japanese pronunciation rules (4): geminate consonants (sokuon)
Japanese is a language that places great importance on mora timing: in Japanese words, each kana takes one beat. The geminate consonant is written with the small
“っ” (katakana “ッ” in loanwords). The geminate is not pronounced in the word, but it takes up one
beat of rhythm; therefore, when you encounter a geminate in a word, you need to pause for one beat before pronouncing the next sound. In romaji, geminates
are written by doubling the consonant letter after the geminate, e.g. roppongi (六本木).

Grammar Notes
1. N は N です。 <noun-predicate sentence>
「は」 is the “topic particle” in noun-predicate sentences, used to mark the subject/topic of the sentence; it is read “wa”.
Because 「は」 marks the topic, it usually has no direct English translation.

The sentence-final 「です」 is the “copula”, equivalent to “am/is/are”, much like the verb “be” in English. At the same time, ending a sentence with 「です」 also conveys the speaker's polite tone toward the listener.
② 李さんは中国人です。／Li is Chinese.
2. N は N ではありません。 <negative form of the noun-predicate sentence>
「ではありません」 is the negative form of 「です」, equivalent to “is not”. The 「では
in 「ではありません」 is mostly used in formal settings such as speeches or in writing; its colloquial form is
① 私は学生ではありません。／I am not a student.
② 佐藤さんは会社員ではありません。／Sato is not a company employee.
③ ジョージさんはイギリス人じゃありません。／George is not British.
This lesson focused on the expressions of noun-predicate sentences in the polite non-past tense. Summarized in the ta-
Table 5-1: Conjugation table of noun-predicate sentences in the polite non-past tense
Tense | Affirmative | Negative
Present/Future | 学生です。 | 学生ではありません。
Past | 学生でした。 | 学生ではありませんでした。
(In spoken language, 「では」 can be replaced by 「じゃ」)
3. Sentence + か。 <question>
The particle 「か」 attached to the end of a declarative sentence forms a question, like the question mark in English. In writing,
Japanese questions generally do not use “?” but end with “。” instead. 「か」 can be attached to a declarative sentence
to form a yes-no question; such sentences are usually answered with 「はい」 or 「いいえ」.
A question word can also be added to form a wh-question; the respondent answers directly according to the meaning of the question word.
When 「か」 marks a question, the sentence is read with rising intonation.
① A: （あなたは）山田さんですか。／Are you Yamada?
B: はい、そうです。／Yes, I am.
② A: 山田さんは学生ですか。／Yamada, are you a student?
B: いいえ、（私は）学生じゃありません。／No, I'm not a student.
③ A: 経済学部の先生はどなたですか。／Who is the teacher in the economics department?
Adding 「か」 to a declarative sentence can also express confirmation; in this case the sentence is read with falling intonation.
① A: あのう、李由加です。／Um..., I'm Li Yuka.
B: あ、李さんですか。／Ah, it's Li.
② A：あの方は社員じゃありません。社長です。／That person is not a staff member. He's
the company president.
B: 社長ですか。／The president, I see.
② A：ジョージさんはアメリカ人で、経済学部の三年生です。／George is Ameri-
can, and a third-year student in the economics department.
B: そうですか。／I see.
4. N で、N です。 <noun conjunction (continuative form)>
“で” is the continuative form of “です”, used to connect noun sentences. In this lesson, when two noun-predicate
sentences share the same subject, they can be joined into one sentence with “で”, and the subject of the second clause can be omitted. Here,
the two clauses are in a sequential relationship. Between Japanese clauses, the comma “、” is generally used
rather than “，”.
① ジョージさんはアメリカ人で、 留学生です。／George is American, and an international
student.
② こちらは中村さんで、日本人です。／This is Nakamura, who is Japanese.
③ あの方はイタリア人で、デザイナーです。／He/She is Italian, and a design-
er.
5. N の N <possession>
The particle “の” placed between two nouns indicates possession or an attributive relation, like “'s” or “of” in English.
① ジョージさんは経済学部の学生です。／George is a student in the economics department.
② 由加：あの方は中村さんの先生ですか。／Is that person your teacher, Nakamura?
中村：はい、そうです。私の先生です。／Yes, that's right. He's my teacher.
③ 李さんは大学院の一年生です。／Li is a first-year graduate student.
6. Sentence + ね。 <confirmation (sentence-final particle ね-1)>
The particle “ね” attached to the end of a sentence expresses the tone of “seeking confirmation” from the listener. It is one of the more
commonly used “sentence-final particles” in Japanese — particles used at the end of a sentence. When “ね” expresses “confirmation”,
it is read with rising intonation and a crisp feel.
① こんにちは。中村さんですね。／Hello. You're Nakamura, right?
② A: 紹介します。こちらは佐藤さんです。／Let me introduce you. This
is Sato.
B: 初めまして。佐藤さんですね。／Nice to meet you. You're Sato, right?
Expression Expansion
1. Subjects in Japanese
Compared with Chinese or English, Japanese usually omits subjects such as “I”, “you”, and “he/she”. For ex-
A: Are you Yamada?
B: Yes, I'm Yamada.
In Japanese, this would more often be expressed as:
It would generally not be said this way:
Japanese also rarely uses the second person “あなた” (you). If you must refer to “you”,
people generally address the other person directly by name, adding “さん”, or use their title such as “先
生” or “社長”, as a sign of respect. For example:
（△）これはあなたのですか。／Is this yours?
（◯）これは中村さんのですか。／Is this yours, Nakamura?
When addressing others, regardless of their gender or age, you can add “さん” after their name to show
respect, e.g. “中村さん”, “ジョージさん”. But when introducing your own name, you must not
add “さん” to your own name.
／Ah, is it Li? Nice to meet you. I'm Nakamura Eri. Hello.
由加：こんにちは。中村さんですね。／Hello. You're Nakamura, right?
In addition, third-person words such as “彼” and “彼女” are not often used either. Although “彼” means “he”,
it can also mean “boyfriend”; although “彼女” means “she”, it can also mean “girlfriend”.
So how should you express “he/she”? Generally, you can add “さん” after the person's name,
such as “李さん”, “中村さん”. If you don't know the person's name, you can also use “あの方”
for the third person, or use the person's title directly, such as “先生”, “社長”, instead of “彼”
“彼女” — and this is more polite.
② A: あの方はどなたですか。／Who is that person?
2. Useful expressions for first meetings in this lesson
(1) When you take the initiative to approach and speak to someone
When you take the initiative to approach someone, you can use “あのう” followed by what you want to say.
“あのう” is a filler word Japanese people often use, equivalent to “um...”. When talking with strang-
ers, you can start with “あのう” to avoid sounding abrupt. But it is not recommended to overuse it, or you will
sound long-winded.
① A: あのう、中国の方ですか。／Excuse me, are you Chinese?
② A: あのう…／Um...
B: はい、何ですか。／Yes, what is it?
(2) The “three-step self-introduction” for first meetings
When meeting someone for the first time, you should first introduce yourself. A simple self-introduction in Japanese
can follow this order:
Step 1: greeting
Step 2: introduce who you are
Step 3: exchange pleasantries
A self-introduction is usually given to someone you don't know, or in fairly formal settings,
so for the greeting part you can choose “おはようございます”,
“こんにちは”, or “こんばんは” depending on the time of day.
In addition, add “初めまして”. “初めまして” is the greeting for a first meeting, with the
meaning “nice to meet you (please treat me well)”.
When introducing yourself to others, note that you must not add the honorific “さん” or titles such as “社
長” or “部長” to yourself. You can use the following sentences to introduce yourself; sentence ② is more po-
lite and humble than ①.
You can also briefly introduce basic facts about yourself as appropriate, such as nationality, age, etc. For example:
③ （私は）経済学部の新入生です。／I'm a new student in the economics department.
④ （私は）中国から来ました。／I come from China.
The particle “から” means “from”. “来ました” means “came”; “ました”
follows a verb to form its past tense. This sentence means “I came from China”. Here too,
the subject “私は” is omitted.
Finally, as a closing, add “please treat me well”. All three of the following mean “please treat me well”,
but with slightly different tones: in general you can use ②; if great politeness is not needed,
use ①; for very formal occasions requiring a very polite tone, use ③. When the other person asks you to treat them well,
you can reply with ④.
① （どうぞ、）よろしく。／Please treat me well.
② （どうぞ、）よろしくお願いします。／Please treat me well.
③ （どうぞ、）よろしくお願いいたします。／Please treat me well. (most polite)
④ こちらこそ。／Likewise — the pleasure is mine.
(3) Introducing a third party
When introducing a third party to someone, you can first say “紹介します”, then give the specific introduction.
“紹介します” is a verb sentence meaning “let me introduce”. Japanese often omits the subject; the same is true in verb
sentences — here the subject “私は” is omitted, and the sentence consists only of the verb “紹介します”.
Next, when giving the specific introduction, you can gesture toward the person being introduced while saying “〇〇
さんです”; the subject can be omitted here. If you don't omit the subject, you can use the pattern “こちらは〇〇
さんです”. “こちら” means “this person”, with a polite, formal tone.
① 紹介します。（こちらは）ジョージさんです。／Let me introduce you. (This
is) George.
This is a common reply for taking up what the other person said in conversation, equivalent to “is that so?”. “そうです
か” can be said with falling or rising intonation at the end. Generally, the final intonation falls,
taking up the other person's statement and meaning “I see” (as in example ①). When the final intonation rises, it expresses
doubt about what the other person said (as in example ②). For example:
① A: ジョージさんはアメリカ人で、経済学部の三年生です。／George is American, a third-year student in the economics department.
B：そうですか。（↘）／I see.
B：そうですか。（↗）／Oh really?

3. The continuative form of adjectives <adjective ren'yokei>
The “continuative” in Japanese, also called “ren'yokei”, is “the form for connecting predicates”. The “continuative” is used at pause points
within a sentence, where the parts before and after the pause are mostly in a parallel, sequential relation. Sometimes we use two, three, or even more
adjectives to describe the qualities of the same thing. When these adjectives are in a parallel relation, the continuative
form of the adjective (i.e. its second ren'yokei) is needed. Different types of adjectives have different continuative forms, as follows:
Type I adjectives: A い → く + て, ...
Type II adjectives: A + で, ...
① 映画の主人公は背が高くて、魅力的です。／The movie's protagonist is tall and attractive.
② 昨日の試験問題は複雑で、難しかったです。／Yesterday's exam questions were complicated and difficult.
Note: the continuative form is chosen according to the part of speech of the first item only, not determined by the second. For example:
③−1 映画の主人公は背が高くて、かっこいいです。／The movie's protagonist is tall and cool.
③−2 映画の主人公は背が高くて、魅力的です。／The movie's protagonist is tall and
very attractive.
“背が高い” is a Type I adjective; whether it is followed by a Type I adjective (like “かっこいい” in ③-1)
or a Type II adjective (like “魅力的” in ③-2) does not affect the continuative form of “高い”. That is, the continuative form of the first item “背が
高い” is determined solely by its own part of speech and is unaffected by what follows.
In addition, tense is determined by the sentence-final predicate; the continuative part does not need to mark tense. For example:
④ 昨日の映画の主人公は背が高くて、魅力的でした。／The protagonist of yesterday's movie was
tall and attractive.
4. N まで <end point>
The particle “まで” follows a noun and indicates an end point, equivalent to “until; up to; as far as”. “まで”

can follow a noun with temporal meaning or a time noun, as in this lesson, or a place noun to indicate the end point of a location. “まで” can also be followed directly by the copula “です” to end the sentence, forming a noun-predi-
cate sentence.
① わたしは昨日、遅くまで日本語の試験でした。／Yesterday my Japanese exam went until late.
② 今日の授業はここまでです。／That's all for today's class.
③ あの歌手のライブツアーは来月20日までです。／That singer's concert tour runs until the
20th of next month.
5. 全然 + adjective (negative)
Like “あまり” learned in the previous lesson, “全然” is also a degree adverb and must be paired
with the negative form of an adjective; it can be translated as “(not) at all ...”.
① A: 昨日の試験は難 しかったですか。／Was yesterday's exam difficult?
B: 全然難しくなかったですよ。／It wasn't difficult at all.
② わたしは運動が全然好きではありません。／I don't like exercise at all.
③ 彼女の料理は全然美味しくありません。／Her cooking isn't good at all.
In spoken language, “全然” alone can also express “not at all”, “none at all”.
④ A: 日本語の試験は難 しかったですか。／Was the Japanese exam difficult?
B: ううん、全然。／Not at all.
The particle “とか” follows a noun and is used to give examples. “とか” is mostly used in spoken conversation; it can be used once in a sentence
or appear multiple times in the same sentence. When “とか” is used, the topic/subject particles “は”
and “が”, and the object particle “を”, can be omitted.
① A: どんな飲み物が好きですか。／What drinks do you like?
B: ミルクティーとか、コーラとか。／Milk tea, cola, things like that.
② 木曜日の午後以降とかはどうですか。／How about, say, Thursday afternoon or later?

2. About making suggestions
(1) Suggestion method 1: N はどうですか。<suggestion II>
Without using a verb, you can make a suggestion with the pattern “N はどうですか”. Here
N is the content of the suggestion, such as the time of an appointment, its content, or some recommended options. It means “How about ...?”.
① 来週はどうですか。／How about next week?
② 6時はどうですか。／How about 6 o'clock?
③ お茶はどうですか。／How about some tea?
④ 映画はどうですか。／How about a movie?
Review: Lesson 9 also covered another use of “N はどうですか” — do you remember it? (See
Lesson 9, Grammar 5 for details)
(2) Suggestion method 2: (いっしょに) N をしましょうか。
We have not yet formally studied the use of Japanese verbs; for now you can memorize the pattern “(いっ
しょに）〜をしましょうか” — “しましょうか” means “shall we (do together)?”.

The particle “を” marks the object of “do”. Attached to an action noun, it conveys inviting or suggesting doing something together, translated as “let's (do together) ...”. Here N is mostly a noun with
verbal meaning, such as “テニス”, “ダンス”, “勉強”.
① 映画の後、一緒にお茶をしましょうか。／After the movie, shall we go get some-
thing to drink together?
Here, “お茶をしましょうか” means “shall we have something to drink?”.
3. Ways to respond to suggestions
(1) Agreeing
You can use the following sentences to express agreement with the other person's suggestion. Depending on the situation, you can add “ありがとう
ございます / thank you” to thank them for the suggestion or invitation.
① A：一緒にテニスをしましょうか。／Let's play tennis together.
② はい、大丈夫です。／Yes, that's fine.
③ そうしましょう。／Let's do that.
Japanese people also use the following sentences when declining a suggestion or invitation, such as “大丈夫で
す。”, “けっこうです。”, “ちょっと……”, “いいです。”, usually accompanied by an apologetic look
or a “すみません” of regret. Depending on the situation, you can also make another suggestion in return, for example:
① A：お茶はどうですか。／How about some tea?
B：あ、大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。／Ah, I'm fine. Thank you.
② A：明日、一緒に映画はどうですか。／How about seeing a movie together tomorrow?
convenient. Next time for sure (let's go together).
“今度” means “next time”. “ぜひ” is an adverb meaning “by all means; definitely”. After “今度はぜひ一緒
に”, the verb “映画を見る / watch a movie” is omitted. The particle “は” emphasizes the tone of “next time for
sure”. So even before you can use the specific verb, you can still use “今度
はぜひ一緒に” to mean “(not this time, but) next time let's definitely do it to-
gether”.

“よかった” is the past form of the adjective “いい”. Adding
the exclamatory particle “ね” after “よかったです” expresses happiness about what happened to the other person;
it can be translated as “That's great”, “Good for you”.

A：よかったですね！おめでとう。／That's great! Congratulations.

The adverb “なんとか” means “(though not as satisfying as hoped) somehow manageable”.
In spoken language, “なんとか” can be used alone or with a verb after it

lowing forms:
“より” is a case particle indicating the standard of comparison. This pattern says that N has more of the characteristic

explained in the predicate than B, Japanese often uses the adverb “ずっと”, translated as “much ...”.
① 中国は日本より広いです。／China is bigger than Japan.
／(This computer) has much more memory than the one from before.

This pattern is a variant of Pattern 1, meaning that compared with N, N has more of the characteristic
shown by the predicate. “ほう” can also be written “方”; it is a noun meaning “a certain side/direction”. “BよりA
のほうが〜” can be translated as “A is more ... than B”. Likewise, this pattern can also serve as the answer to Pattern 4
questions.
① 日本より中国のほうが広いです。／Compared with Japan, China is bigger.
② パソコンよりスマホのほうが値段が高いです。／Compared with computers, smartphones are
more expensive.
The adverbial particle “ほど” follows a noun and indicates degree. When followed by a negative, this pattern says N does not have
the characteristic to the same degree as N. “Bは A ほど〜 (negative)” can be translated as “B is not as ... as A”,
“B doesn't ... as much as A”.
① 日本は中国ほど広くありません。／Japan is not as big as China.
② パソコンはスマホほど値段が高くありません。／Computers are not as expensive
as smartphones.
This pattern is the question form of comparison sentences. It asks which of N and N has more of the characteristic
shown by the predicate. “A と B とどちら（のほう）が〜か” can be translated as “Which is (more) ..., A or B?”.
When choosing between the two, the answer usually uses the Pattern 2 form, with the “B より” part mostly omitted —
just answer “A のほうが〜”.
① A： 中国と日本とどちら（のほう）が広いですか。／Which is bigger, China or
Japan?
B：中国のほうが広いです。／China is bigger.
② A：パソコンとスマホとどちらが高いですか。／Which is more expensive, a computer or a smartphone?
B：スマホのほうが高いです。／The smartphone is more expensive.
The suffix “−さ” can attach to the stem of Type I adjectives and some Type II adjectives to form a noun,
indicating degree or state. For example:
複雑 ([II-adj] complicated) → 複雑さ ([noun] complexity; degree of complexity)

1. N が〜 <object (case particle が−3)>
Besides marking the subject, the particle “が” can also mark an object. In this lesson, “が”
marks the object of a certain ability or aptitude. Such ability-related words mainly consist of Type II adjectives (such as
“上手”, “下手”, “得意”, “苦手”, “好き”, “嫌い”) and verbs (such as “できます”, “わ
かります”).
Type II adjectives
上手／下手
得意／苦手
Verbs
① 私は運動が嫌いです。／I don't like sports.
② 辛いものが苦手です。／I can't handle spicy food.
③ 兄は歴史が得意です。／My older brother is good at history.
④ 先生の話がよくわかりません。／I don't quite understand what the teacher says.
⑤ 父は料理ができます。／My father can cook.
2. （N の中で）N がいちばん〜 <particle “で”: scope>
In Lesson 11 we learned several forms of Japanese comparison sentences. Here we learn the “superlative” form of adjective-predi-
cate sentences, expressing that within the scope shown by N, N has the most of the characteristic shown by the
predicate. The particle “で” after a noun delimits the scope; the adverb “いちばん” means “most”.
1 The “superlative” is an important point in English grammar: among three or more things or people, one has the most of some quality.
Here, the Japanese “superlative” corresponds to the “comparison” patterns of Lesson 11.
This pattern can be translated as “(among ...N...) N is the most ...”.
① 日本の漫画の中で、『スラムダンク』がいちばん好きです。／Among Japa-
nese manga, I like Slam Dunk the best.
I like basketball the most.
③ クラスの中で、李さんがいちばん 頭 がいいです。／Li is the smart-
est in the class.
④ 日本料理の中で、お寿司がいちばん好きです。／Among Japanese dishes,
I like sushi the best.
3. N なので、〜 <cause-effect −2>
The particle “ので” connects two clauses in a cause-effect relationship. In this pattern, when the first clause is a
“noun-predicate sentence” (see Lesson 5, Grammar 1), it can be joined directly in the form “N+な＋ので”;
this pattern can be translated as “because (it is) ...N..., ...”. Compared with “から”
from Lesson 9 (see Lesson 9, Grammar 4), “ので” tends to emphasize an objectively existing reason, and its tone
is more indirect and formal.
きですよ。／Because I'm from Shonan in Kanagawa Prefecture, I also love Slam Dunk
② 雨なので、運動会は中止です。／Because of rain, the sports day is cancelled.
③ 学生なので、お金がないです。／Because I'm a student, I have no money.
4. 〜は〜が、〜は〜。 <contrast (particle は–2)>
In compound sentences expressing a contrastive relation, when the two clauses are similar in form and carry a sense of contrast,
the subjects of both clauses are marked with the particle “は”.
ます。／I can't play basketball, but I can play a little soccer and tennis.
② 日本語は 上手ですが、英語は下手です。／My Japanese is good, but my English is
poor.
③ 昨日は寒かったですが、今日はとても暑いです。／Yesterday was cold, but to-
day is very hot.
④ 私 は学生ですが、 妹 は会社員です。／I am a student, but my younger sister is a com-
pany employee.
5. N に〜 <object of a state or quality>
The particle “に” follows a noun and indicates the object of the ability, attitude, quality, etc. that follows. After “に”
come mostly adjectives expressing quality, state, ability, etc.
① マスクは外出に必要です。／Masks are essential for going out.
② 横の 中国語訳は日本語学習 に便利です。／The Chinese translation beside it is convenient for learning
Japanese.
③ 兄は中国の歴史にも、日本の歴史にも詳しいです。／My brother knows both Chinese his-
tory and Japanese history well.
④ 駅の近くのアパートは、買い物に便利です。／The apartment near the station is convenient for
shopping.
6. 〜の（／ん）です。 <explanation −1 (adjectives, nouns)>
Pattern: N + な + の（／ん）です。
The pattern “〜の（／ん）です。” is very common in spoken Japanese; it can follow the “attributive form of an adjective”
or “noun + な”; in speech, the form “〜んです。” is mostly used. It expresses
a personal assertion, or an explanation of a situation. “〜の（／ん）です。” is hard to translate directly and is generally left untranslated. The specific functions and use
scenarios of the pattern “〜の（／ん）です。” are summarized below:
(1) Explaining a situation or giving a reason
Used to explain the “cause or reason” of what was stated before; mainly for the speaker's “explanation” of their situa-
tion. For example:
① 実は『キャプテン翼』も『テニスの王子様』も好きなんですよ。／Actually, I love both Captain
Tsubasa and The Prince of Tennis.
② すみません、今はちょっと 忙しいんです。／Sorry, I'm a bit busy right now.
③ 私は冷たい飲み物が苦手なんです。／I don't handle cold drinks well.
(2) Acceptance and realization
The situation described in the preceding text becomes the reason for the following “〜の（／ん）です”
sentence; the pattern “〜の（／ん）です” expresses the speaker's “acceptance” of that result,
with a sense of acknowledging and realizing the validity of one's own inference.
④ 由加さんは本当に漫画ファンなのですね。／Yuka, you really are a manga
fan.
(3) Stating the background of a topic, for indirect suggestions or requests
You can use “〜の（／ん）です” to state the background of a topic in order to make an indirect sug-
gestion or request. Here, “〜の（／ん）です” is mostly connected with the situation to be stated
afterward. This usage mostly appears in the form “〜の（／ん）ですが、〜”.
⑤ 新しいパソコンがほしいのですが。／I'd like to buy a new computer...
⑥ マックの最新モデルがいちばん軽いのですが。／The latest Mac model is the lightest...
⑦ あのう、テレビの音が大きいのですが。／Um, the TV is a bit loud...
Example ⑤ is a common expression when describing your specific needs to a shop assistant while shopping.
Example ⑥ uses the pattern “〜の（／ん）です” to explain to the other person, thereby imply-
ing “how about considering this one?”. Example ⑦ likewise indirectly explains the situation to express the speaker's implied request: could you turn the volume down?
1. Degree adverbs that can modify adjectives
Degree adverbs that can modify adjectives include “超”, “とても”, “ちょっと”, “少し”, “あ
まり”, “全然”, etc. Among these, “超” has the highest degree and is mostly used in speech (example ①). In writing or
formal situations, “大変”, “非常に”, etc. can be used (example ②).
“ちょっと” and “少し” are similar in meaning, both indicating a small quantity of things or actions, a low
degree — like “a little; slightly”. “ちょっと” is used more in spoken language.
“あまり” must be followed by a negative form, meaning “(not) very ...” (example ③).
“全然” also needs to be followed by a negative form, translated as “(not) at all ...” (example ④). But in
modern Japanese society, “全然” can also be followed by an affirmative, with basically the same meaning as “とても” or “非常に”,
though this usage is generally not used in formal speech or business settings (example ⑤).
① 話のスピードが超速いです。／The speaking speed is super fast.
② 清華大学は 中 国で非常 に有名です。／Tsinghua University is very famous in China.
③ ここの家賃はあまり安くないです。／The rent here isn't very cheap.
④ イタリア語が全然わかりません。／I don't understand Italian at all.
⑤ A：忘年会、金曜日はどうですか？／How about Friday for the year-end party?
2. Other common spoken expressions in this lesson
Adding the prefix “お” before “上手” describes someone else being “good at something”. This
phrasing is more polite and is mostly used by women. Of course, “お上手” cannot be used about yourself.
The adverb “さすが” can be followed by a noun to emphasize that something fully matches one's prior expectation or judgment,
equivalent to “as expected of ...”, “truly worthy of ...”.
Three stars. The food is tasty and beautifully presented. The service is good too.

2. Question word + も <total negation>
A question word followed by the particle “も” and used with a negative predicate expresses total negation,
equivalent to “no ... at all”, “not any ...”.
