3. Question word + か <indefinite>
A question word followed by the particle “か” expresses indefiniteness. This usage is not limited to questions; it
can also be used in declarative sentences. Note that when “question word + か” is used in a question, it
forms a yes-no question, and the answer usually starts with “はい” or “いいえ”.
① あのレストランにお 客 さんが何人かいます。／There are a few customers
in that restaurant.
② 特に重要な理由がいくつかあります。／There are several particularly important reasons.

The particle “から” can follow nouns indicating time, place, or order, marking the starting point of time, place,
or sequence — like “from ...” in English. “から” can also be followed directly by the copula
“です” to form a noun-predicate sentence.
① 体のトレーニングは明日からです。／Physical training starts tomorrow.
② 今から成績の発表です。／The announcement of grades starts now.
③ ここからはテストの内容です。／From here on is the content of the test.
The starting-point “から” can also be paired with the end-point particle “まで”.
④ 会議は今月の4日から6日までです。／The meeting is from the 4th to the 6th of this month.

(1) Plain forms of noun-predicate sentences and adjective-predicate sentences
Japanese mainly has two speech styles: “polite” and “plain”. The plain style, as opposed to the polite style, is mostly used in conversations between friends
or family, or in written forms such as novels and papers. When using Japanese, you need to choose the appropriate
style according to the relationship between the two parties.

(2) Switching between polite and plain styles in speech
The speech style in spoken Japanese changes according to the listener, the situation, and the topic. One such situa-
tion is that even in a mainly polite-style conversation, the plain style can be used when the speaker voices their own feelings (such as surprise or emer-
gency). The “本当だ！”, “やばい！”
and “じゃ、図書館だ！” in this lesson's model dialogue are Nakamura's self-talk when feeling surprised or flustered, and therefore

When borrowing something from someone, Japanese people generally use this phrase as a courtesy. It is a polite expression,
meaning “let me borrow this”.
① A：そこの自転車、お借りしますね。／That bicycle — I'll borrow it, okay?
Japanese people have set greetings for leaving and returning. When about to leave (home, the office, etc.),
they say “行ってきます。”, meaning “I'm off”, “I'll be back”. The people staying behind
reply “行ってらっしゃい”, equivalent to “take care; see you later”.
In addition, upon returning they say “ただいま。 (I'm home)”, and the people at home (or in the office)
respond with “お帰りなさい。” (welcome back).
① (about to leave) 息子：行ってきます。／I'm off.
② (coming back in) 息子：ただいま。／I'm home.

Classifying verbs by their conjugation type is the first step to efficiently mastering verb sentences. Traditional Japanese
school grammar and the more recently popular Japanese textbooks classify verb conjugations slightly differently, but mostly
they differ only in the names of the types. Here we summarize the conjugation types of Japanese verbs with their Japanese names, morphological features,
and example words in Table 14-1. The “dictionary form” of a verb is also called the “basic form” or “plain
form” — the original form in which a verb appears as a dictionary entry, without any conjugation.

When Japanese verbs are used, the polite suffix “ます” is added after the dictionary form.
When the verb takes the suffix “ます”, the verb's form changes according to its conjugation class;
this change is called “verb conjugation”.
The specific rules for the change before “ます” are as follows:
Change the final u-row kana of the verb to the corresponding i-row kana, then attach “ます”. For example:
Remove the final kana “る” of the verb, then attach “ます”. For example:
寝る：ねる＋ます＝寝ます

② Kuru-verb: “来る”. Change “来る” to “来”, then attach “ます”. That is:
来る：来る→き＋ます＝来ます
In addition, the verb stem that remains after removing “ます” is called the
“masu-stem of the verb”, marked in this book's grammar notes as “V ます形” (in Japanese school grammar also called “動

4. Time + ごろ
The suffix “ごろ” after a specific time noun expresses an approximate time, translatable as “about;
around”. “ごろ” can also be written “頃”. When a time noun is followed by “ごろ”, the particle
“に” marking the point in time can be omitted.
① いつも夜 1 1時ごろ寝ます。／I always sleep around 11 pm.
② 今日は2時ごろに帰ります。／I'm going home around 2 today.
③ 3月ごろ、桜が咲きます。／The cherry blossoms bloom around March.
④ 2000年ごろから、車が多くなりました。／From around 2000, cars
increased.
In Japanese, “〜くらい（ぐらい）” can follow quantity words for time, money, count, etc.,
expressing an approximate number — like “about; around” in English.
① 発表は全部で２時間ぐらいでした。／The presentation was about two hours in total.
② 食費は毎月３万円ぐらいです。／Food expenses are about 30,000 yen a month.
③ 教室には学生が5人ぐらいいます。／There are about 5 students in the classroom.
6. なる <change>
Pattern: N + に + なる
“なる” is one of the verbs that best embodies the characteristics of Japanese, used to describe the natural change of things, or of their qual-
ities and states. “なる” can be combined with nouns, adjectives, verbs, and other parts of speech.
This lesson mainly covers the use of “なる” with nouns and adjectives. The specific joining rules are as follows:
Noun: N + に + なる Example: 会社員 → 会社員になる
Type I adjective: A（い）→ く + なる Example: 寒い → 寒くなる
Type II adjective: A + に + なる Example: 静か → 静かになる
① 1 1月の初めから寒くなります。／It gets cold from the beginning of November.
② 体調が大分よくなりました。／My physical condition has improved a lot.
③ 日本語がかなり上手になりました。／My Japanese has become quite good.
④ 今週末のイベントは 中止になりました。／This weekend's event has been cancelled.
⑤ でも、午後から眠くなるから、何もできなくなります。／But from the afternoon on I get sleepy,
so I can't do anything.
Example ⑤ “何もできなくなります” means “(become) unable to do anything”. The
“できない” in the sentence is the negative form of the verb “できる (can; to be able to)” (covered in detail in Lesson
17). When “できない” is followed by the verb “なる”, the negative “ない” changes to
“なく” before “なる” to express change.

Lesson 10's “Expression Expansion” 3 briefly introduced the use of the “（いっしょに）Nをしましょう
か” pattern and how to respond. Here we explain the use of “V ましょう。/V ましょうか。” in de-
tail. “ましょう” after the masu-stem of a verb expresses an invitation, suggesting that the other person do something together with you.
It is often paired with the adverb “いっしょに”, equivalent to “let's ... (together)”.
Adding the interrogative particle “か” after “V ましょう” softens the tone further,
with the feel of asking for the other person's consent.

1. Japanese transitive/intransitive verbs and the particle “を” <“を”: marking the object>
Japanese verbs can be divided into intransitive and transitive verbs. Intransitive verbs cannot take an object, much like
“intransitive verbs” in English. Transitive verbs can take an object, much like the English “transitive verb” concept. Of
course, some individual Japanese verbs have both intransitive and transitive properties.
When using a transitive verb, the particle “を” is placed after the noun to mark the object of the verb.
① 本を読みます。／I read a book.
② 資料を調べます。／I look up materials.
When the object part becomes the topic, the particle “は” or “も” can replace “を”.
I send emails, but I don't write letters much.
④ 休みの日は、よく映画を見ます。買い物もします。／On days off I often watch
movies. I also go shopping.
(1) “で” marks <place>
The particle “で” follows a noun indicating a place or location, marking the place where an action takes place, translatable
as “at; in”.
① 伊藤先生のゼミでデータを集めました。／I collected data in Professor Ito's semi-
nar.
② 私はよく喫茶店で小説を読みます。／I often read novels in cafés.
③ 日本では、口頭試験はどんな 準備をしますか。／In Japan, how do you prepare for an
oral exam?
(2) “で” marks <tool, means>
The particle “で” follows a noun and indicates the tool or means used to perform an action, gener-
ally translated as “with; by; using ...”.
① スマホで外国語を勉強します。／I study foreign languages on my smartphone.
② インターネットで資料を調べます。／I look up materials on the internet.
③ 日本人はお箸で料理を食べます。／Japanese people eat with chopsticks.
(3) “で” marks <cause, reason>
The particle “で” after a noun can also indicate a cause or reason, translated as “because of ...”.
① 中村さんは毎日、試験勉強 で大変なんですよ。／Nakamura has a hard time every day be-
cause of exam preparation.
② 病気で学校を休みました。／I was absent from school because of illness.
③ 地震で電車が止まりました。／The trains stopped because of the earthquake.
3. N に <object of an action>
The particle “に” follows a noun and marks the target of the following action.
① 中村さんにメールで資料を送ります。／I send materials to Nakamura by email.
② 午後、ジョージさんに会います。／I'm meeting George in the afternoon.
③ 友達に簡単なやり方を聞きます。／I ask a friend for an easy way to do it.
“なら” is also called a “topic-highlighting particle”; attached to a noun, it highlights that noun as the topic.
So what kind of nouns can be highlighted by “なら”? Generally, something the other
person just said, a topic discussed before, or something predictable from the context can all be
brought up as the topic. The “英語なら” in this lesson's dialogue belongs to the first case. “N なら、〜” corre-
sponds to “if it's ... (N), then ...” in English.
① 日本語の小説なら、家には何冊かありますよ。／Speaking of Japanese novels,
I have several at home.
② A：新しいパソコンがほしいんですが。／I'd like a new computer...
B：パソコンなら、こちらがいいですよ。／If it's computers, this one is good.
③ A：一緒に喫茶店に行きましょうか。／Shall we go to a café together?
B：コーヒーなら、スタバのがいいですね。／If it's coffee, Starbucks is
good.
“について” follows a noun and is used to bring up a topic, translated as “about; regarding”. “について”
can be followed by “です” to form a predicate sentence, or by a predicate sentence with a verb.
① 経済のグローバリゼーションについてです。／It's about economic globalization.
② 先週 の旅行について作文を書きました。／I wrote an essay about last week's
trip.
③ 今日の授業 について、何か質問はありますか。／Do you have any questions about today's
lesson?
1. About offering help
When you want to proactively offer help or do something for someone, you can use the following two ways to
express it.
(1) V ましょう／V ましょうか <volition, suggestion (V ましょう–2)>
In Lesson 14 we already learned the invitational use of “V ましょう”, i.e. suggesting that oth-
ers do something together with you. Besides invitation, “V ましょう” can also be used to proactively offer help
to someone, expressing the speaker's offer to perform an action themselves.
“か” carries a questioning tone; “V ましょうか” has the feel of seeking the other person's consent and is softer than
“V ましょう”. When using this pattern, the subject is mostly first person (usually omit-
ted), and the beneficiary of the action is mostly the listener.
① A：手伝いましょうか。／Shall I help you?
B：すみません。お願いします。／Sorry to trouble you. Please do.
② A：荷物を持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry your luggage?
B：大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。／I'm fine. Thank you.
③ メールでは時間がかかりますから、電話をかけましょうか。／Email
takes too long, so let me give them a call.
Besides “V ましょう／V ましょうか”, you can also use “協力します。” to more di-
rectly express your willingness to help. Note that when the first person does a favor for the second person,
or does something for them, there is no need to specifically point out for whom it is done. So just using the verb 「協
力します」 expresses “I'll help (you)”.
It's the real performance soon. We won't have time to prepare.
B：そうですか。協 力しますよ。／I see. I'll help you.
2. How to respond when someone offers help
When you are willing to accept the help offered, you can use the following sentences.
① A：それ、持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry that for you?
B：助かります。ありがとうございます。／That's a great help. Thank you.
② A：それ、持ちましょうか。／Shall I carry that for you?
The “助かります。” in example ① means “to be helped; to be saved”. When someone offers
to help, you can use “助かります。” to express gratitude.
The “お願いします” in example ② is a polite expression you can use when asking someone to do something for you,
translated as “please; I'm counting on you”.
If you need to decline the other person's kind offer, you can first thank them and then use the following sentence.
B：あ、大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。／Ah, I'm fine. Thank you.
3. Describing the sequence of actions or situations
You can place conjunctions such as “まず”, “それから”, “そして”, “その後”, and “最後に” at the
head of sentences to describe the sequence of actions or situations. These words mean “first”, “then”, “moreover”,
and “finally” respectively.
① まず、自分でテーマを考えます。／First, think of a topic yourself.
② それから、原稿を書きます。／Then, write the script.
③ そして、辞書で単語の読み方を調べます。／Also, look up the readings of words in a dictionary.
④ 最後に、たくさん練習します。／Finally, practice a lot.

The particle "に" follows the verb masu-stem or an action noun (for suru-verbs, just the stem)
and is followed by a movement verb to express the purpose of the movement. Can be translated as "go (to a place) to ..."

⑤ 資料を届けに来ました。／(I) came to deliver the materials.

equivalent to "... while ..." in English.

3. Quantifier + も <subjectively many>
A quantifier followed by the particle "も" shows the speaker subjectively considers the amount large. In example ①, un-
der normal circumstances three students is not many, but when the speaker feels three students is a lot,
"も" can be added after the quantifier "3人" to convey the speaker's subjective sense that the number
is large.
① 教室に学生が3人もいます。／There are (as many as) three students in the classroom.
② 議論は3日も続きました。／The discussion lasted (a whole) three days.
③ 日系企業を５社も訪問しました。／(We) visited (as many as) five Japanese companies.
The "何冊" appearing in this lesson's dialogue, although an interrogative word, is also a quantifier. When the inter-
rogative quantifier "何冊" is followed by the particle "も", even though the number is indefinite, it carries the sense
of subjectively regarding it as many; it is not a question.
④ あの映画は何度も見ましたよ。／I've seen that movie many times.

adjective + でしょ（う）

ょ" form is more common. Can be translated as "... right?"

that purpose".

The ko-so-a-do words are four groups of demonstratives beginning with こ, そ, あ, and ど respectively,
used to point to things, places, or directions (see Table 6-1), translatable as "this ...", "that ..."
"that ... (over there)", and "which ...". Although both "so-series" and "a-series" words can be rendered "that ...",
they must be distinguished in actual use.
When the speaker and listener are far apart, the speaker uses "so-series" words for things or directions closer to the
listener. "A-series" words generally refer to third-party things or directions far from both the speaker and the
listener.
Table 6-1: ko-so-a-do demonstratives
Things  Places  Directions
Proximal これ ここ こちら
Medial それ そこ そちら
Distal あれ あそこ あちら
Interrogative どれ どこ どちら
① A：それは何ですか。／What is that?
B：（これは）日本のお菓子です。／(This is) a Japanese sweet.
② A：中村さんのかばんはどこですか。／Where is Nakamura's bag?
B：あ、あそこです。部屋の中です。／Ah, over there. Inside the room.
③ A：ここは何のお店ですか。／What kind of shop is this?
B：ここはパン屋です。／It's a bakery.
Besides indicating direction, こちら / そちら / あちら / どちら can also refer to
places, people, or things, and are more polite and formal than これ / ここ / どれ / どこ.
④ A：あのう、すみません。お手洗いはどこですか。／Excuse me. Where is the
restroom?
B：こちらです。／This way.
When introducing someone, こちら is also used to be polite.
⑤ 紹介します。こちらは李さんです。／Let me introduce (you). This is Li.
The particle も follows a noun and means "also". Note that when も marks the topic of a sentence,
it replaces は.
① 中村さんの部屋もここですか。／Is Nakamura's room here too?
② 張さんも中国人です。／Zhang is also Chinese.
③ 私もこの大学の学生です。／I am also a student at this university.
「と」 is a particle of coordination, used to connect two or more nouns in a parallel relationship.
Usually translated as "and".
① 清華大学と北京大学は 中国の大学です。／Tsinghua University and Peking University are Chi-
nese universities.
② ここは李さんと中村さんの 教室です。／This is Li and Nakamura's classroom.
③ これは由加さんのユーザー名とパスワードです。／This is your (Yuka's) user-
name and password.
4. N (place) に N が あります／います。 <existence sentence I>
This is the basic pattern of the "existence sentence". The particle に follows "N (place)" to mark the
"place of existence", like "in/at ..." in English. The particle が marks the subject that exists (N). The verbs あ
ります and います both mean "to exist", like "there is/are". Their negative
forms are ありません and いません. あります is mostly used for things that cannot move on their own;
います is used for animate beings such as people or animals that can move on their own.
① 1階にコンビニがあります。／There is a convenience store on the 1st floor.
② 教室に学生がいます。／There are students in the classroom.
③ 駅の近くに中村さんのアパートがあります。／Near the station is Nakamura's apartment.
5. N (place) には N が あります／います。 <existence sentence II>
The particle は marks the topic. Generally, a Japanese sentence can take a part other than the predicate verb
and promote it to the topic of the sentence by adding the topic-marking particle. In the basic pattern "N (place) に N が
あります／います。", to make the place where something exists the topic of the sentence,
add the topic particle は after "N (place) に", giving the pattern:
N (place) には N が あります／います。 <existence sentence II>
① かばんには携帯があります。／There is a phone in the bag.
② コンビニの隣にはパン屋があります。／Next to the convenience store is a bakery.
6. N は N (place) に あります／います。 <existence sentence III>
To make the thing that exists (i.e., the subject) the topic of the sentence, replace the subject particle が
with the topic particle は, giving the pattern:
N は N (place) に あります／います。 <existence sentence III>
① あのう、Wi-Fiはありますか。／Excuse me, is there Wi-Fi?
② 由加さんの部屋は、３階にあります。／Yuka's room is on the 3rd floor.
"N は N (place) に あります／います。 <existence III>" can also be interchanged with the previously learned
"N は N です" pattern, mostly in spoken style. Compared with "〜は〜にありま
す／います", "N は N です" simply omits the existence verb ありま
す or います, but the meaning is basically the same.
③ −1 A：あのう、病院はどこですか。／Where is the hospital?
B：銀行の前です。／In front of the bank.
③−2 A：あのう、病院はどこにありますか。／Where is the hospital?
B：銀行の前にあります。／It's in front of the bank.
④ −1 社長は今、会議室です。／The president is in the meeting room now.
④−2 社長は今、会議室にいます。／The president is in the meeting room now.
"それから" is a conjunction. As an independent word, a conjunction generally connects preceding and following sentences,
paragraphs, or words. "それから" generally has two meanings: one follows a preceding item and indicates
that the following item happens next, usually translated "then"; the "それから" in this lesson
expresses addition, equivalent to "also; in addition" in English.
① それから、これはわたしの携帯番号です。／Also, this is my phone number.
② それから、これ、ほんの気持ちです。／And also, this is just a small token.
③ 中村さん、李さん、それから、小林 さんは大学院生です。／Nakamura,
Li, and also Kobayashi are graduate students.

2. Ways to end a conversation
Japanese people generally don't use "さようなら" when saying goodbye, because it has the nuance of
"farewell forever". Japanese people choose an appropriate way to end a conversation depending on the context. Here, using the patterns from this lesson
as examples, we explain a few common situations.
This is a common Japanese greeting meaning "thank you for your hard work". お疲れ様でした is the past
form, used to show appreciation after someone has worked hard. Note that this greeting is generally not used
toward people of higher status. When it comes up in conversation, you can reply like this:
B：お疲れ様でした。（used between people of similar age or standing）／Thanks for your hard work.
B：ありがとうございました。（used toward someone of higher status）／Thank you.
"ゆっくり" is an adverb meaning "slowly; at leisure". "休んでください" is made of the verb 休む
(to rest) plus the auxiliary てください meaning "please (do)". The ね at the end of the sentence
is a modal particle. The sentence means "please get some good rest".
Of course, if it is at night before bed, you can also use "お休みなさい"
(good night), learned in Lesson 1.
"ありがとうございました" is the past tense of "ありがとうございます", and is also
a common greeting for parting on formal occasions. Japanese people generally don't say "さ
ようなら" when parting, because "さようなら" is too formal and can imply "farewell forever". Instead,
you can end the conversation with "ありがとうございました", carrying the sense of "thank you very much for today".
3. Common expressions for giving small gifts
In daily work and life, Japanese people have the custom of giving small gifts to those who look after them.
These gifts are usually small local specialties. Japanese people are very reserved when expressing feelings,
often saying "ほんの気持ちです" while handing over the gift. It means "(this is) just a little
token of my appreciation".

3. Interrogative + が <marking the subject>
The case particle が follows a noun to mark the "subject". When an interrogative word is the subject,
it must be marked with が, and the answer must also use が. When an interrogative is the subject, the particle
は cannot be used.
① A：研究室に誰がいますか。／Who is in the lab?
B：マイケルさんと先生がいます。／Michael and the teacher are there.
② どれが李さんのスマホですか。／Which one is your (Li's) phone?
③ A：どなたが（×は）日本語の先生ですか。／Who is the Japanese teacher?
B：あの方が（×は）日本語の先生です。／That person is the Japanese teacher.
4. Japanese "pre-noun adjectivals" (rentaishi)
"この" "その" "あの" "どの" are "pre-noun adjectivals" and cannot be used independently. They can only precede a
noun, indicating and qualifying the person or thing referred to; they belong to the ko-so-a-do word family.
① 弟 さんはどの大学にいますか。／Which university is your brother at?
② 私の部屋はあの建物の2階です。／My room is on the 2nd floor of that building.
"Pre-noun adjectival" is one of the Japanese parts of speech. As the name suggests, it is "a word that connects to a substantive".
That is, a substantive (i.e., a noun) must follow it. For example:
The Japanese for "This is my computer" should be:
③-1. （○）これは私のパソコンです。／This is my computer.
In ③-2, "この" is a pre-noun adjectival, so a substantive must follow it, not the particle は. As for "this
computer is mine", the Japanese is:
④-1. （○）このパソコンは私のです。／This computer is mine.
"This computer" must be formed with the pre-noun adjectival この followed by パソコン, while in ④-2 "こ
れ" and "パソコン" are both substantives and cannot be connected.
The particle だけ follows a noun or quantifier to express limitation; can be translated as "only", "just".
① A：経営学部の留学生は何人ですか。／How many international students are there in the business school?
B：5人です。アジア人は、私だけです。／There are five. The only Asian is my-
self.
③ 朝ごはんはりんごだけでした。／Breakfast was only an apple.
6. N の N <appositive>
In previous lessons we learned to use の to connect two nouns, expressing possession (e.g., 私の本)
or attribute (e.g., 日本語の本). In this lesson, の expresses an appositive relation between nouns,
meaning the nouns before and after の refer to the same thing. In apposition, the noun before の usually denotes a relation-
ship or property, while the noun after の is usually a proper noun, such as a person's name.
① そして、 弟 のハチです。／And this is my little brother, Hachi.
② こちらは課長の長谷川さんです。／This is section chief Hasegawa.
③ 紹介します。クラスメートのジョージさんです。／Let me introduce (him). (This)
is my classmate George.

The particle よ is used at the end of a sentence to express the speaker's assertion, declaration, and other emphatic nuances. The sentence-final
よ is mostly read with rising intonation.

B：10年前の写真ですよ。／It's a photo from 10 years ago.
② A：中村さんもこの大学の学生ですか。／Is Nakamura also a student at this university?
1. Japanese family terms and introducing family members
In Japanese, when it comes to one's family situation, inside and outside must be clearly distinguished. For the other party's situation
use respectful terms; for your own, use humble terms. This distinction between respectful and humble terms effectively
avoids modifiers like "your" and "my", which fits the Japanese habit of rarely using 私 or あなた,
and also makes the language more concise and polite.
Before some nouns made of two kanji — "Sino-Japanese words" — the prefix ご can be added
as an honorific or to show respect, mostly referring to the listener's situation, e.g. ご意見 (your opinion), ご
住所 (your address). "Your family" can be said directly as ご家族. As in this lesson's dialogue, it can also be expressed as 李さんのご家族 or 中村さんのご家族.
(2) Kinship terms
Kinship terms in Japanese also require special attention. For other people's family members use respectful terms, and
for your own relatives use humble forms. Table 7-3 summarizes Japanese kinship terms in three
cases: "humble" is used when introducing your own relatives to people outside the family, as in example ①;
"in-family address" is what family members use to address each other, as in example ②; "respectful"
is what people outside the family use to address someone's relatives, as in example ③.

1. N を <marking the object>
The particle を follows a noun to mark the object. Japanese is an SOV (subject-object-verb)
language, where the predicate verb usually comes at the end of the sentence and the object comes earlier, marked with
を.
"ください" is the imperative form of the verb くださる (to give), equivalent to "please give me
...". "Nをください。" is mostly used when shopping or ordering food.
① 水族館の入 場券をください。／I'd like an admission ticket to the aquarium, please.
② チーズバーガーセットをください。／I'd like a cheeseburger set, please.
To express "I also want ...", use the particle も meaning "also". も and を
cannot be used together; も must replace を.
④ それから、ホットコーヒーもください。／And also, a hot coffee please.
2. N を (quantity) ください。
To express the quantity you want to buy, place the quantifier before the verb ください. For
quantifier expressions, see this lesson's "Expanding Expressions" 1-(2).
① A：この水族館の入 場 券を3枚ください。／Three admission tickets to the aquarium, please.
B：はい、3000円です。／Certainly, that will be 3,000 yen.
② チーズバーガーセットを一つください。／One cheeseburger set, please.
③ A：いらっしゃいませ。／Welcome.
B：あのう、これを2本ください。／Um, two of these, please.
④ シャツを３枚ください。／Three shirts, please.
In Japanese, quantifiers generally come before the verb. For example:
⑤ 兄が2人います。／I have two older brothers.
⑥ スマホが２台あります。／There are two phones.
The verb お願いします in this pattern means "I beg; please" and is a courteous, polite
expression; when asking someone to do something for you, お願いします can directly re-
place a specific verb. In examples ① and ②, お願いします replaces the verb ください.
① ホットコーヒーをお願いします。／A hot coffee, please.
② これを4つお願いします。／Four of these, please.
The particle で follows a noun to indicate the means or method of the following action. Combined with お願いします,
it forms the means by which you ask someone to do something.
In this lesson's "Model Conversation" pattern (example ③), the object-marking case particle を
is replaced by で. The particle で after a noun marks the "state". Example ④ rather emphasizes
pointing out "I want a small coffee". Example ③ appears in a conversational context, where a hot coffee
has already been mentioned. So when asked "what size?", answering "Sサイズで" emphasizes that the way of buy-
ing the coffee is the small size. This expression is more idiomatic and natural. Also:
⑤ （when paying）アリペイでお願いします。／Please (process the payment) with Alipay.
⑥ （when asking the other party to contact you）Eメールでお願いします。／Please contact me by email.
The assertive auxiliary でございます is the formal version of です. Formal style is mostly
used on formal occasions such as speeches or international conferences, or by service-industry staff toward customers. When used,
the subject is generally oneself or one's own side's people or things; it generally cannot be used for the respected listener
or their people or things.
① エレベーターはこちらでございます。／The elevator is this way.
② 私が担当者でございます。／I am the person in charge.
③ （when Tanaka's colleague introduces their own manager to the client company）部 長 の田中でご
ざいます。／This is Manager Tanaka.
④ A（person from an outside company）：田中部長は、今日、お休みですか。／Is Manager Tanaka off
today?
B（Tanaka's colleague）：はい、休みでございます。／Yes, he is off today.
The interrogative どう is equivalent to "how". なさいます is the honorific verb for する
(to do); using なさいます makes the speaker's tone more polite and formal.
"どうなさいますか" is equivalent to "How would you like it?" "What would you like to do?"
mostly used by service-industry staff. For example:
would you like?
B：Lサイズでお願いします。／A large, please.
When the interrogative どう serves as the predicate, it can be followed by ですか to form the wh-question "〜はどうで
すか。", used to ask the listener's opinion about the thing the subject refers to. For example:
② このコーヒーはどうですか。／How is this coffee?
③ 清華大学はどうですか。／How is Tsinghua University?
④ 最近はどうですか。／How have you been lately?

2. Common expressions for shopping, ordering, and paying
(1) Step 1: State your needs
When ordering at a restaurant or shopping at a store, you can use "Nをください。" to say "I'd like ..."
"please give me ..." to state your needs. You can also use the pattern "Nをお願いします。", which
is more polite and courteous.
② ヨーグルトをお願いします。／Yogurt, please.
(2) Step 2: State the means or method of fulfilling your needs
After stating your needs, if you want to add the means by which you want them fulfilled, you can use "Nで
お願いします。".
① コーヒーはSサイズでお願いします。／For the coffee, a small size please.
② （when asking the clerk to wrap a gift）リボンはゴールドでお願いします。／For the rib-
bon, gold please.
(3) Step 3: Payment
You can use an action noun followed by "お願いします。" to politely ask
someone to do something for you. For example:
① 客： お会計、お願いします。／The check, please.
You can also use "Nでお願いします。" to state the payment method. For example:
② 現金でお願いします。／(I'll pay) in cash.
④ アリペイでお願いします。／(I'll pay) with Alipay.
When paying in cash, the receiver usually says "〜円のお返しです" when giving change.
3. Common replies in this lesson to requests or instructions from others
To respond positively to a request or instruction, you can use "わかりました。" or "はい、わ
かりました。" — meaning "Understood", "Got it".
B：はい、わかりました。／Yes, understood.
This is a set phrase, translatable as "Understood", "Certainly". It is mostly used by subordinates giving a positive reply
to a superior's instruction. It is more formal and polite than "わかりました。", and is mostly used by service-industry staff.
"はい" has many uses in Japanese; it can express affirmation, as in example ①. In this lesson's conversation, "は
い" is said while handing money to the other party, with the nuance of drawing their attention, as in examples ② and ③.
① A：新入生ですか。／Are you a new student?
B：はい。／Here you go.
③ はい、私の名刺です。／Here, this is my business card.
"大丈夫です。" originally means "no problem; it's all right". In recent years, modern Japanese has derived
another new usage: declining someone's invitation or kind offer, mostly used by young
people.
① （when the clerk asks whether you have a points card and offers to add points）大丈夫です。／No thanks, I'm fine.
② （when a friend offers you snacks but you don't really want any）ありがとう、大 丈 夫で
す。／ Thanks, I'm fine.

1. Adjective predicate sentences
Adjectives as predicates express states or constant properties. In Japanese, adjectives are divided into two types: type I
adjectives (ending in い) and type II adjectives (in Japanese "school grammar" type II adjectives are called "adjec-
tive verbs"). The polite non-past forms of adjective predicate sentences differ according to the type:
(1) Polite non-past (present or future) affirmative forms of adjective predicate sentences
Type I adjective: A ＋ です。
Type II adjective: A ＋ です。
(2) Polite non-past (present or future) negative forms of adjective predicate sentences
Type I adjective: A い→く＋ありません。
Type II adjective: A ＋では（じゃ）ありません。
Table 9-1: Non-past conjugations of adjective predicate sentences (polite form)
(example: 静か)
① 東京は寒いです。／Tokyo is cold.
② あの映画は面白くありません。／That movie is not interesting.
③ 先生は親切です。／The teacher is kind.
④ 日本語は簡単ではありません。／Japanese is not simple.
Note that the adjective いい must first be changed to よ
い before conjugating. For example, the non-past negative form of いいです is よ
⑤ 成績はよくありません。／(My) grades are not good.
This is a typical expression favored by Japanese speakers, unlike what Chinese speakers are used to. The particle
は marks the topic of the sentence (also called the "big subject"), and が marks the subject (the "small subject"). In the pattern "A は
B が X です", the statement is mainly about the topic A (A is usually the whole of a person or thing),
B is usually a part of A, and "B が X です" expresses A's characteristic. For example:
① 象 - 鼻 - 長い → 象は鼻が長いです。／Elephants have long noses.
② 富士山 -形 - いい → 富士山は形がいいです。／Mt. Fuji has a nice shape.
③ 今日 -天気 - いい → 今日は天気がいいです。／The weather is nice today.
④ 彼女 -性格 - 明るい→ 彼女は性格が明るいです。／She has a cheerful personality.
The degree adverbs あまり and そんなに can both be paired with the negative form of adjectives,
equivalent to "not very ...", "not that ..." in English.
① A：東京は寒いですか。／Is Tokyo cold?
B：いいえ、あまり寒くありません。／No, it's not very cold.
② 日本語はそんなに難しくありません。／Japanese is not that difficult.
③ このパソコンはそんなに遅くありません。／This computer is not that slow.
4. Sentence + から。 <cause-effect>
The particle から is used at the end of a sentence to express a reason, equivalent to "because ..." (sentence)
① （中村さんは）とても真面目ですから。／Because (Nakamura) is very serious.
② アイスクリームがいいです。暑いですから。／Ice cream would be nice. Because it's hot
(outside).
5. N は どうですか。 <asking about the nature of things>
The interrogative どう means "how". "N は どうですか" is used to ask about
the nature of something or the listener's view of what the subject refers to; it can be answered with an adjective predicate sentence.
① A：日本の留学生活はどうですか。／How is life as an international student in Japan?
B：順 調ですよ。／It's going well.
② A：日本語はどうですか。／How is Japanese?
B：難しいです。／It's hard.
③ A：この映画はどうですか。／How is this movie?
6. Sentence + よ。 <assertion; calling attention>
The particle よ is used at the end of a sentence to express the speaker's assertion or declaration, an emphatic nuance.
② 山羊座の人はみんな真面目ですよ。／Capricorns are all serious, you know.
③ 日本語はそんなに難しくありませんよ。／Japanese isn't that hard, you know.
7. Sentence + ね。 <mild exclamation (particle ね II)>
When the particle ね at the end of a sentence expresses mild exclamation, it is read with falling intonation; depending on the nuance, it can also be lengthened
to ねえ.
① 由加ちゃんはすごいですね。（↘）／Yuka, you're amazing.
② この洋服、かわいいですね。（↘）／These clothes are cute, aren't they.
③ 由加ちゃんのこのスマホケース、かわいいですね。（↘）／Yuka, this phone case of yours
is so cute.

1. Plain forms of verbs
Lesson 13 covered the plain forms of nouns and adjectives. Like noun sentences and adjective sentences, verb-final
verb sentences also have corresponding polite and plain forms.
Among them, "Vる (verb dictionary form)", and "Vない" and "Vなかっ
た" related to the verb imperfective form will be detailed in Grammar 2 and 3 of this lesson. Here the polite and plain forms of verbs are summarized in
Table 17.
Table 17-1: Four-quadrant comparison of polite and plain verb sentences
Affirmative  Negative
Present  Polite: V ます。  Polite: Vません。
Future  Plain: Vる (verb dictionary form)  Plain: Vない。
Polite: V ました。  Polite: Vませんでした。
Plain: V た。  Plain: Vなかった。
Polite style is mostly used in formal settings; its tone is formal and courteous, so it is also called "polite style" — in Japanese,
"丁寧語". In spoken settings, plain style sounds more casual and intimate and is mostly used in conversations among friends or family;
in written settings, plain style emphasizes a more argumentative or declarative tone, so in writing it
is mostly used for papers, news reports, and the like.
2. V る (verb dictionary form)
The affirmative plain form in the Japanese non-past tense is the verb's "dictionary form", also called the "verb original
form" or "verb basic form". This is the most basic form of the verb; since dictionary entries appear in this
form, it is usually called the "dictionary form". For example:
① 敬体：スマホでウェブサイトを閲覧します。／Browse websites on a phone.
简体：スマホでウェブサイトを閲覧する。／Browse websites on a phone.
② 敬体：よく徹夜します。／Often stay up all night.
简体：よく徹夜する。／Often stay up all night.
3. V ない (verb imperfective/nai-form)
The negative plain form of a verb is formed by attaching the negative auxiliary ない to the verb.
Generally called the "nai-form" or "negative form" of the verb, also the "imperfective form".
The rules for attaching ない to verbs are as follows:
Change the final kana of the verb from the u-row to the a-row, then add ない. Note that
for type I verbs ending in う, change the final う to わ before adding ない.
Remove the final kana る, then add ない. For example:
① Suru-verb: する. Change する to し, then add ない. That is:
② Kuru-verb: 来る. Change 来る to 来, then add ない. That is:
来る：来る→こ＋ない＝来ない
Note that the negative form of ある is not あらない, but the adjective な
① この週末は家に帰らない。／(I'm) not going home this weekend.
② 今の学生はあまり運動しない。／Students these days don't exercise much.
The plain form of "V ませんでした" is the past tense of "V ない", i.e., "V なかった".
③ 宿題が多くて、昨夜、あまり寝なかった。／There was so much homework that I barely slept last night.
④ A：昨日のビールは？／What about yesterday's beer?
B：冷蔵庫だよ。／In the fridge.
A：ビールは冷蔵庫になかったよ。／The beer wasn't in the fridge.
4. Verb attributive form
A verb can also modify a noun as an attributive modifier, called the "verb attributive form" — the form of a verb connecting to a
substantive (noun). The verb attributive form is exactly the same as the verb's plain form; choose the appropriate form according to the
tense and meaning. For example:
① 授業の予習や復習、課題をやる時間。／Time for class preparation and review, and for doing assignments.
② 明日行く場所はどこですか。／Where is the place (you're) going tomorrow?
③ 雨なので、飛行機が飛ばない可能性があります。／Because of the rain, the plane may
not fly.
5. N (period) に N (quantity) V <frequency>
The particle に follows a noun expressing a period (usually a time span), indicating the frequency or quantity
of an action within that period. Equivalent to "per ..." in English.
① 週に3回運動する。／Exercise 3 times a week.
② ２か月に1回ぐらい映画を観る。／Watch a movie about once every two months.
③ 1年に1回中国へ帰る。／Go back to China once a year.
6. N についての N <about>
In Lesson 15 we learned "Nについて", which follows a noun to introduce a topic, translatable as "about
...". "Nについて" can also be followed by の to qualify noun 2. Can be translated as "about
① こちらは大学生のライフスタイルについてのアンケートです。／This
is a survey about university students' lifestyles.
② このウェブサイトには、来 週 の口頭試験についての 情 報はない。／
This website has no information about next week's oral exam.
③ 来週は期末試験なので、明日から経済学についての本を読む。／Because
the final exam is next week, (I) will start reading a book about economics tomorrow.
As an adverb, ほとんど is mostly paired with the negative form of verbs. Can be translated as "hardly
(not) ...". Similar in usage is the adverb あまり, which can also be paired with the negative form of verbs
and can be translated as "(not very) ...".
① インターネットや SNS はほとんど利用しません。／Hardly use the internet
or social media.
② 漫画はときどき読みますが、アニメはほとんど見ません。／I read manga from time to
time, but I hardly watch anime.
③ Eメールはあまり使いません。／Don't use email much.
④ 梅雨の季節はあまり晴れません。／It rarely clears up during the rainy season.
8. N + particle + の + N
Besides directly connecting two nouns (e.g., 私の車, 日本語の
本), the possessive particle の can also follow certain particles with concrete meanings (such as で, と, から, へ,
まで), combining with them to modify a noun. For example:
友達と食事する → 友達との食事
大学の授業などに出席する → 大学の授業などへの出席
Note that there is no "N にの N" form. To express "toward ... (destination, direction) ...",
use the form "N への N".
① 雨の影響で、外国からの観光客が減少しました。／Due to the rain, foreign
tourists have decreased.
② 後輩との食事会はとても楽しかったです。／The dinner with my juniors was very
enjoyable.
Due to the typhoon, the flight to Hong Kong was cancelled.
The particle や is used to list two or more things, and など means "etc.". The
two can be used together in the form "N や N など", translatable as "... and ... etc.". They can also
be used separately.
① インターネットやSNSなど／internet, social media, etc.
② A：デパートに何がありますか。／What is in the department store?
B：映画館や本屋などがあります。／There's a movie theater, a bookstore, and so on.
③ A：いつもどこで服を買いますか。／Where do you usually buy clothes?
B：ユニクロやタオバオで買います。／I buy them at Uniqlo, Taobao, etc.
1. お/ご + N <prefixes>
"お" and "ご" are both prefixes. "お" is mostly attached before native Japanese words, showing respect for the listener or a third
party, or referring to things related to the listener, such as お名前 or お国. It can also
express the speaker's polite tone, as in お店 or お知らせ.
"ご" is mostly attached before Sino-Japanese nouns, or action-related Sino-Japanese words, showing respect for the listener or the person in the topic.
For example: ご両親, ご利用, ご協 力.

Both the "verb ta-form" and the "verb dictionary form" can be followed by 時（に） to mean "at the time of
...". But note that the time points expressed by the "verb dictionary form" and the "verb ta-form" differ.
"V る時（に）" refers to something that happens while the preceding action is not yet complete (example ①), while "V た時
（に）" refers to something that happens at the point after the preceding action is complete (examples ②③).
① 友達の家に遊びに行く時に、お土産を買いました。／When (I) was about to go to a friend's house

when (we) went to hang out, everyone made dumplings together.

2. V たことがある <experience>
"Verb ta-form" followed by ことがある expresses having had a certain experience, translatable as "have (once)
...". The negative form of this pattern is "V たことがない" (example ②). Also, when answering "〜
たことがありますか", you can use ある or ない.
① あの人は、確か前に会ったことがあります。／That person — I think I've met
(them) before.
② 日本で歌舞伎を見たことがありません。／I have never seen kabuki in Japan.
③ A：体育の授業で怪我をしたことがありますか。／Have you ever been injured in PE class?
B：はい、あります。／Yes, I have.
④ A：着物を着たことがありますか。／Have you ever worn a kimono?
B：いいえ、ありません。／No, I haven't.
The "V たことがある" pattern is mostly used for experiences long past or once had; it is not used to nar-
rate recent experiences (example ⑤).
⑤ ×私は、昨日、お寿司を食べたことがあります。
○私は、昨日、初めてお寿司を食べました。／I ate sushi for the first time yesterday.
3. V る/V ないことがある <sometimes; occasionally>
In contrast to "V たことがある", the "verb dictionary form" or "verb nai-form" followed by "こと
がある" expresses that the action or situation sometimes occurs, translatable as "sometimes do/don't ...", "(occasionally)
there are times when ... / times when not ...".
① いつも寝る前にシャワーを浴びますが、朝起きてからシャワーを浴び
ることもあります。／I usually shower before bed, but sometimes
I shower after getting up in the morning.
② 梅雨の季節では、一週 間も晴れないことがある。／During the rainy season, sometimes
there isn't a single sunny day for a whole week.
③ 兄とは仲がいいのですが、喧嘩することもありますよ。／I get along well with my brother, but we
sometimes fight too.
④ ここの地域は、半年以上も雨が降らないことがある。／In this region, there are times when it
doesn't rain for more than half a year.

Pattern: V plain form + でしょう
A (i-adjective) plain + でしょう

A plain-style sentence (but for type II adjectives and nouns, drop the だ) followed by でしょう ex-
presses the speaker's conjecture, translatable as "... probably", "I suppose". The intonation of でしょう usually falls; it is often paired with adverbs like た
ぶん (probably) or きっと (surely). Its plain form is だろう.
① 初めは難しいでしょうね。／It must be hard at first.
② 明日は雨でしょう。／It will probably rain tomorrow.
③ ご両親もあなたの結婚を反対するでしょう。／Your parents will probably oppose your mar-
riage too.
④ 今頃はもうホテルに着いているだろう。／By now they should have arrived at the hotel.
8. 〜間、〜 <during ...>
Pattern: N の間、〜
"〜間" expresses two states or actions continuing in parallel — that is, throughout the whole period
described in the first clause, the action in the second clause continues. The first clause can be a noun + の or "verb ている"
followed by 間, and the second clause usually ends with "V ていた". Can be translated as "during ..., (all along) ...".
① 夏休みの間、ずっとアメリカを旅行していました。／During the whole summer vacation (I) was
traveling in America.
② 母がご飯を作っている 間 、 私 はずっと横で手伝っていました。／While my mother was cooking, I kept
helping beside her.
③ バスを待っている間、ずっとスマホを見ていました。／While waiting for the bus, (I) kept
looking at my phone.
9. かな <modal particle>
The modal particle かな combines the question particle か with the exclamatory particle な.
Attached after a plain sentence or a noun, it expresses a question with a light exclamatory nuance, or an uncertain
tone when talking to oneself.
① かなりきつい仕事なので、あの人は一人でできるかな。／This is pretty demanding work — I wonder if he
can do it alone.
② もうそろそろ向こうに着くころかな。／I guess we'll be arriving (there) pretty soon.
③ 締め切りは確か来月の4日かな。／The deadline was the 4th of next month, if I remember right.
"さあ" is an interjection used to get the listener's attention and urge them to do something. For example:
① さあ、出発しましょう。／All right, let's go!
② さあ、見てください。／Come on, take a look!
When visiting a Japanese home, you usually take off your shoes at the entrance and step up one level before entering. There-
fore, the verb used for entering a room is 上がる. Besides 上がってください, an even more polite way to say "please come in"
is お上がりください. Of course, for places where you don't need to remove your shoes, such as offices
or shops, you can also use 入ってください or お入りください.
This is a polite phrase meaning "excuse me for intruding". It is used when entering someone's private space, such as the host's
room or office.

B：はい、どうぞ。／Yes, please come in.

In Lesson 18 we learned the verbs あげる/くれる/もらう for expressing the giving and receiving of things.
This lesson covers the use of these giving/receiving verbs after て as auxiliary verbs. Verbs
followed by てあげる/くれる/もらう express the giving and receiving of actions. The specific rules are as follows:
<Giving/receiving verb sentence I>
N (I / giver) は N (receiver) に V てあげる
<Giving/receiving verb sentence I> expresses doing something for someone else. When neither N nor N is "I",
only two relationships are possible between N and N:
・N and N are at the same psychological distance from the speaker.
・The speaker is psychologically closer to N.
Note, however, that the "V てあげる" pattern over-emphasizes that you deliberately did something for the other person,
which can make the listener feel they are being done a favor. So if the other person is not someone close to you,
avoid it as much as possible to prevent sounding rude (example ③). In such cases use "V ましょうか"
(example ④), which is more polite.
① 観光客に道を教えてあげます。／(I'll) give directions to the tourists.
た。／Yuka made delicious Chinese food for her classmates.
③ （×）先生、重いので、持ってあげます！
④ （○）先生、重いので、持ちましょうか。／Teacher, it's heavy — shall I
carry it for you?
<Giving/receiving verb sentence II>
N (giver) は N (I / receiver) に V てくれる
<Giving/receiving verb sentence II> expresses that someone else does something for you or for someone on your side,
i.e., "(someone) does ... (for me)". Here the giver of the action is the subject, and the receiver (usually "I")
is marked with に, but 私に is often omitted.
⑤ 日本人の友達が作文を直してくれました。／My Japanese friend corrected my ess-
ay.
⑥ 母は1人で私を育ててくれました。／My mother raised me all by herself.
<Giving/receiving verb sentence III>
N (I / receiver) は N (giver) に/から V てもらう
<Giving/receiving verb sentence III> expresses receiving someone's doing something for you. The subject of this pattern
is the receiver of the action, i.e., "I", and 私は is often omitted. The giver of the action is usually marked with に
or から. Both "V てくれる" and "V てもらう" can express that the speaker receives someone's doing some-
thing for them, i.e., the speaker is the beneficiary. But compared with "V てくれる", "V てもらう" more often
carries the nuance of being fortunate to "receive" someone's doing something for you. It therefore better highlights the speaker's gratitude
toward the giver of the action.
The trains and buses had all stopped, so a friend drove me there.

1. Verb potential form
The verb potential form expresses "can (do something)". The "can" expressed by the Japanese potential form
is close to "can" in English, and likewise expresses two meanings: (1) someone has a certain
ability, or (2) the conditions for doing something are met.
The conjugation rules for the verb potential form are as follows:
Type I verbs: change the final u-row kana to the corresponding e-row kana, then add る.
Type II verbs: drop the final kana る, then add られる. For example:
辞める：やめる＋られる＝辞められる
寝る：ねる＋られる＝寝られる
① Suru-verb: change する to できる. That is:
② Kuru-verb: change 来る to 来, then add られる. That is:
来る：くる→来＋られる＝来られる

the object is usually changed to が. For example:

this is quite common in informal spoken language and is called
"ra-dropping words" (ら抜き言葉) in Japanese. For example:
⇒ 私 は明日授業 があるので、来（ら）れません。／I have class tomorrow, so I can't come.

1. あげる/くれる/もらう <Giving/receiving verbs>
Unlike Chinese, Japanese uses different words for "give" depending on the subject. The most
representative are "あげる", "くれる", and "もらう". This set of verbs expresses the giving and
receiving of things, and they are called "giving/receiving verbs". The specific rules are as follows:
Ⅰ. N (giver/I) は N (receiver) に N (thing) をあげる
"あげる" means "to give". It is used when "I" give something to someone else. When neither N is
"me", only two relationships are possible between the two Ns:
・Both Ns are at the same psychological distance from the speaker (as in example ②).
・The speaker feels psychologically closer to one N (as in example ③).
① （わたしは）彼女に花をあげました。／I gave my girlfriend flowers.
ます。／In Japan, girls give boys chocolate on Valentine's Day.
③ 妹 が友達にお土産をあげました。／My younger sister gave her friend a souvenir.
Besides "あげる", "やる" also means "to give", and its usage is basically
the same as "あげる". "やる" tends to emphasize giving to people of lower status than the speaker (such as one's
younger siblings) or to things (such as flowers, birds, pets). However, it is rarely used in modern Japanese.
④ 花に水をやります。／Water the flowers.
Ⅱ. N (giver) は N (receiver/me) に N をくれる
"くれる" also means "to give". But unlike "あげる", "くれる" refers to
someone else giving something to "me" (as in example ⑤). Therefore, the subject must always be "someone else". When
neither N is "me", only one relationship is possible: compared with one N, the speak-
er feels psychologically closer to the other N (as in example ⑥).
⑤ お 正 月に祖父がお年玉を（わたしに）くれました。／At New Year's, my grand-
father gave me New Year's gift money.
⑥ 社長が 妹 に花をくれました。／The company president gave my younger sister flowers.
Ⅲ. N (receiver/I) は N (giver) に/から N をもらう
"もらう" means "to receive". It expresses that "I" receive something from someone. For receiving
from someone, the "giver" is followed by the particle "に" or "から". When using "もらう",
the subject must be "I" (as in example ⑦). When neither N is "me", only one relation-
ship is possible: the speaker feels psychologically closer to one N than the other (as in the question in example ⑧).
I got advice about the gift from my younger sister.
／What did Xiao Li give you?
"いただく" also means "to receive"; it is the humble form of "もらう". When
the speaker wants to express respect toward the giver, "もらう" can be replaced with "いただく",
which sounds more polite and formal.
⑨ みなさんから素敵なプレゼントをたくさんいただきました。／I received many
wonderful presents from everyone.
In Japanese, different giving/receiving verbs must be used according to person restrictions, and this
is one reason why Japanese often omits the subject. In fact, in Japanese, from the predicate verb alone, together with the
surrounding context, the listener can easily tell who the subject of the sentence refers to.
"たい" follows the masu-stem of a verb to express desire, equivalent to "(I) want to (do)...".
"たい" conjugates according to the rules for i-adjectives.
① あの会社で働きたいです。／I want to work at that company.
② 今日はあまり出かけたくないです。／I don't really want to go out today.
③ 遊びに行きたかったのですが、台風で止めました。／I wanted to go out and have fun, but
I decided not to because of the typhoon.
When the verb is transitive and takes an object marked with "を", that object can also be marked with "が"
instead.
The pattern "V masu-stem + たいです" is fairly strictly restricted by person and is generally used for the first person
(so the subject is often omitted). Also, asking about the second or third
person's wishes with the question form "V たいですか" is not very polite. Especially when the listener is of higher status or not very close to you,
you should try to avoid asking about their wishes with "V たいですか".
⑤ ○ 今日はあの人に会いたくありません。／I don't want to see that person today.
⑥ △ 何が食べたいですか。／What do you want to eat?
⇒ ○ お昼ご飯は何がいいんですか。／What would you like for lunch?
Pattern: V (plain form) + か分かりません。
A (i-adjective, plain form) + か分かりません。
A (na-adjective, plain form) + か分かりません。 (※A だ + か分かりません。)
N (plain form) + か分かりません。 (※N だ + か分かりません。)
A plain-form question containing a question word followed by "分かりません" indicates something you don't know;
equivalent to "I don't know...". A plain-form question is generally formed with the plain form of a verb or i-adjective, or
a noun or na-adjective stem followed by the question particle "か".
① 新幹線の切符をどこで買うか分かりません。／I don't know where to buy Shinkan-
sen tickets.
② いつ雨が降るか分かりません。／I don't know when it will rain.
③ 中村さんの傘はどれか分かりません。／I don't know which one is Nakamura's umbrella.
The particle "ずつ" follows a quantity word or degree adverb, and expresses doing something repeatedly in fixed amounts,
or distributing equally in the same amount or proportion.
① 1人ずつ発言する。／Speak one by one.
② 日本語が少しずつ上手になりました。／My Japanese has improved little by little.
③ みかんを一人3個ずつあげます。／Give each person 3 mandarin oranges.
5. N にする <Choice>
A noun followed by "にする" expresses choosing one thing from among many options. Equivalent to "choose..."
or "decide on...". Often used when ordering food, shopping, etc.
① A：お飲み物はどうなさいますか。／What would you like to drink?
I didn't know which color was best, so I chose one of each color.
③ A：今日のお昼は何にしましょうか。／What shall we have for lunch today?
Ramen. Let's have ramen.
6. Adjective continuative form
Pattern: i-adjective A い→く + V
na-adjective A + に + V
The "adjective continuative form" is the form in which an adjective is followed by an inflecting word (i.e., a verb). With its continuative
form, an adjective can modify a verb, describing the manner in which the action proceeds or how it is carried out. In other words, this
is the adverbial use of adjectives. When an i-adjective is followed by a verb, its final "い" changes to "く"
before the verb; when a na-adjective is followed by a verb, "に" is added to its stem before the verb.
① 皆さんからの質問に親切に答えます。／I answer everyone's questions kind-
ly.
② お皿をきれいに洗いました。／I washed the dishes clean.
③ 早く走りましょう。／Let's run faster.
7. 〜ので、〜 <Cause/result II>
Pattern: V (plain form) + ので、〜
A (i-adjective, plain form) + ので、〜
A (na-adjective, plain form) + ので、〜 (※A だ → な + ので、〜)
N (plain form) + ので、〜 (※N だ → な + ので、〜)
"ので" can be used mid-sentence to state a reason. In Lesson 12 we already learned the use of a noun fol-
lowed by "ので" to state a reason. This lesson further extends the word classes that can precede "ので"
to others: "ので" can also follow the plain form of a verb or i-adjective, or a na-adjective stem,
to state a reason arising from objective circumstances. Note, however, that for nouns and na-adjectives in the first quadrant (i.e., the non-past af-
firmative form), when their plain ending is followed by "ので", "だ" must be replaced with "な",
forming "N なので" or "A なので".
① 頭が痛いので、早く帰りたいです。／I have a headache, so I want to go home early.
② 海外にいるので、参加ができません。／Because I'm overseas, I can't attend.
③ 発音があまりきれいじゃないので、たくさん練習したいです。／Because my
pronunciation isn't very good, I want to practice a lot.
④ ここは、今人気のお店なので、予約が難しいです。／This is a popular
restaurant right now, so it's hard to get a reservation.
The original meaning of "とんでもない" is "completely unexpected, unreasonable". From this it extends to

“おめでとうございます” means “congratulations.” “ございます” is used to express
politeness and can be left untranslated in Chinese. Between very close acquaintances, “ございます” may also be
omitted. Before “おめでとうございます”, you can also add the occasion being congratulated, such as “お
誕生日” (birthday), “ご結婚” (marriage), “ご入社” (joining a company), “ご就 職” (starting a job), etc.
Means “what a relief / thank goodness.” It is mostly an inner exclamation
of joy when something the speaker was worried about did not happen.

*Verbs ending in “ぐ” are followed by “で”
③ For verbs ending in “す”, change “す” to “し”, then add “て”.
④ For verbs ending in “む”, “ぶ”, or “ぬ”, change “む”, “ぶ”, “ぬ” to “ん”,

*The te-form of “行く” is irregular: “行って”

2. V ている ＜continuation of an action (V ている-I)＞
“V ている” has many uses and is a common Japanese pattern. In this lesson, “V ている”
indicates that an action is in progress; it is often used with adverbs like “今” and “ちょうど”, equivalent to the Chinese
“正在……” (“to be doing ...”). “V ている” is the plain form expressing this meaning; its polite form is “ていま
① A: 今、何をしていますか。／What are you doing now?
B: ピアノを弾いています。／I'm playing the piano.
② A: すみません。この問題がわからないのですが。／Sorry, I don't understand this question.
考えましょう。／Actually, I'm thinking about that problem too. Let's think about it together.
③ 今、運転しながら、音楽を聴いています。／Right now I'm listening to music while driving.
Adding “た” to a verb expresses completion, past, etc.; it is the plain form of “V ました”.
The change rules for “V た” are the same as for the verb te-form: just change “て” to “た”. Example:
① 漢字の読み方を間違えた。／I got the kanji reading wrong.
② 鈴木さんはスマホをどこかに落とした。／Suzuki dropped his smartphone somewhere.
③ あっちこっち探したが、見つからなかった。／I looked everywhere but couldn't find it.
4. V て、V て、V ます。 ＜verb continuation (chūdan)＞
When a sentence contains two or more verbs in a sequential relationship,
they are usually connected with “V て”. When several verbs are linked in one sentence, it indicates that the actions occur in sequence;
this ordering need not be translated in Chinese.
① 3時に起きて、勉強しました。／I got up at 3 in the morning and studied.
(I) want to go to Tokyo, and see Tokyo Tower and the Skytree.
③ インターネットで資料を調べて、パワーポイントを作ります。／I'll look up materials online and make a PowerPoint.
④ 朝起きて、シャワーを浴びて、会社へ行きます。／I get up in the morning, take a shower, and go to work.
5. V てください。 ＜request＞
The verb te-form followed by “ください” expresses a request for someone to do something, equivalent to “please ....”
Japanese has many polite expressions, and there are many patterns for making requests. “V てくだ
さい” is mostly used for polite instructions or requests. Therefore, “V てください” is generally not used toward superiors.
Please get some good rest.
② 電話番号を教えてください。／Please tell me your phone number.
③ 明日の10時半に来てください。／Please come at 10:30 tomorrow.
④ これは中国のお土産です。どうぞ、食べてください。／This is a souvenir from China. Please try some.
Pattern: V る＋つもりだ.
The verb dictionary form or nai-form followed by “つもりだ” expresses the speaker's intention, translatable as
“I intend to ...” / “I plan to ....” “V るつもりだ” is fairly strictly limited to the first
person. Using a question with “つもりだ” can sound impolite to the listener, so unless the relationship is close,
it should be avoided (as in example ③).
① この夏休みはノーベル 賞 の受 賞 作品を読むつもりです。／I plan to read Nobel Prize-winning works this
summer vacation.
② 明日からお酒をやめるつもりです。／I plan to quit drinking starting tomorrow.
③ ジョージさん、レポートは何について書くつもりですか。／George, what do you
plan to write your report about?
Also, for “have no intention of doing ...” / “not plan to ...”, use the verb nai-form followed by “つも
りだ”, for example:
④ この冬休みは帰国しないつもりです。／I don't plan to go back to my home country this winter vacation.
7. 〜予定だ。 ＜plan＞
Pattern: V る予定だ.
Compared with the “〜つもりだ” pattern, “V る予定だ” is used to state plans that are basically fixed;
it is relatively objective and does not include the speaker's subjective will. Therefore, there are no strict
person restrictions, the tone is softer, and it can be translated as “plan to (do something)” or “be scheduled to (do something).”
① 李さんはジョージさんと一緒に村上夏樹先生の講演会に参加する予定
です。／Xiao Li and George plan to attend Murakami Natsuki's lecture together.
② 今週の土曜日、歌舞俎を見に行く予定です。／This Saturday, I plan to go see
kabuki.
③ 今回のプロジェクトは２週間の予定です。／This project is scheduled to take two weeks.
④ 明日は朝6時の飛行機に乗る予定です。／I'm scheduled to take the 6 a.m. flight tomorrow.

1. Japanese verb aspect and its polite and plain forms
“V ている” belongs to the category of “aspect (アスペクト)” in Japanese grammar and expresses
the state of an action (such as its continuation or completion). Besides the negative of “V ている”, “V ていない”,
“V ている” can also combine with the past tense to form “V ていた” or “V てい
なかった”. Table 20 summarizes the polite and plain forms related to “V ている”.
Table 20: Four-quadrant comparison of polite and plain forms of “V ている”
Present/future — Polite: Vています。 Polite: Vていません。
Plain: Vている。 Plain: Vていない。
Polite: Vていました。 Polite: Vていませんでした。
Plain: Vていた。 Plain: Vていなかった。
① 朝からずっと曇っている。／It's been cloudy since morning.
② 地震の時、私は庭の掃除をしていた。／When the earthquake struck, I was cleaning the yard.
③ この夏休みは、ずっとマラソンの練習をしていた。／All through this summer vacation I was
training for the marathon.
④ 小さい時は、まだ日本語を習っていなかった。／When I was little, I
hadn't started learning Japanese yet.
2. V ている ＜continuation of a result (V ている-II)＞
In Lesson 19 we learned the first use of “V ている”, expressing the continuation of an action.
This lesson continues with other uses of “V ている”. The second use: attached to instantaneous
verbs, it describes the continuation of the result after the action has occurred.
3. V ている ＜habitual behavior (V ている-III)＞
The third use of “V ている”: it expresses an action repeated over a recent period, habitual
behavior, or an action continued over a long period.
① 弟 は、大学のサークルでジャーナリストをやっています。／My younger brother works as a journalist
in his university club.
② 兄は今、アメリカに住んでいます。／My older brother is living in America now.
③ 今、パリでフランス料理を習っています。／I'm currently learning French cooking in Paris.
④ 彼と毎週会っています。／I meet him every week.
The negative form of the durative “V ている” is “V ていない”; its polite form is “V ていま
せん”. It is often used with the adverb “まだ” and can be translated as “not (yet) ...”.
This pattern is mostly used as a negative answer to “もうV ましたか。” (“Have you already ...?”).
① A: 講演会はもう始まりましたか。／Has the lecture already started?
B: まだ始まっていませんよ。急いでください。／It hasn't started yet. Hurry up.
② A: 部長に電話しましたか。／Did you call the department manager?

“前（に）” attaches to the verb dictionary form (example ①) or after a noun with an action meaning plus “の”
(example ②), and expresses doing some action before the preceding action occurs. It can be translated as “before
..., ...”. The “に” after “前” marks the time point of the following action and can sometimes be omitted.
① 食事をする前に、手を洗いましょう。／Let's wash our hands before eating.
② 食 事の前に、 食 器をテーブルに並べる。／Before the meal, set the tableware on the table.
③ この質問に答える前に、ちゃんと考えてください。／Before answering this question, please think carefully.
6. V てから ＜after ...＞
The verb te-form followed by “から” expresses the sequence of actions and can be translated as “after (doing) ...,
(then do) ....”
① 口コミ情報をチェックしてから、商品を買います。／I check the online reviews first, and then
buy the product.
② 日本でお風呂に入るときは、体を洗ってから、入ります。／In Japan, when taking a bath,
you wash your body first and then get into the tub.
③ 上司に報告してから、レポートを書きます。／After reporting to my boss, I write the report.
7. (third person) V たがる/N をほしがる
In previous lessons we learned “V たい” for wanting to do something (Lesson 18) and “N がほしいです” for wanting
something (Lesson 11), as well as the person restrictions on these two patterns. This lesson covers how
these two patterns are used with the third person.
When expressing a third person's desire to perform an action, the “V たがる” form is generally used.
“-たがる” is a derived verb from “-たい”. Note that with “V たがる”, the verb's object
is marked with “を” and cannot be changed to “が”.
chef of that restaurant.
② 弟 は新しいカメラを買いたがっています。／My younger brother wants to buy a new camera.
“V たがる” expresses the subject's (third person) desire to perform an action; in contrast,
“N をほしがる” expresses the subject's (third person) desire to obtain something.
③ 弟 は新しいカメラをほしがっています。／My younger brother wants a new camera.
Murakami Natsuki's autograph.
“見える” means “can see ....” This is an intransitive verb that inherently carries a potential meaning;
the object of such intransitive verbs is marked with “が”. Another verb with the same usage as “見える” is
“聞こえる”, translatable as “can hear ....”
① あそこの赤い看板が見えますか。／Can you see that red signboard over there?
③ 外はうるさくて、先生の話がよく聞こえません。／It's noisy outside, so I can't hear

④ 後ろの方は聞こえますか。／Can the people at the back hear?
The adverb “わざわざ” means “to go out of one's way (to do something).” In this lesson, “わざわざ” carries
the nuance of “bothering to do (something unnecessary).”

② わざわざ 車 で 5時間もかけて限定 商 品を買いに来た。／(They) drove 5 hours
out of their way just to buy the limited-edition item.
“わざわざ” is also used to comment on others' actions with the positive nuance of “taking the trouble to”, and is often paired with honorific
expressions. In this usage, it cannot be used by the speaker about their own actions. For example:
③ わざわざありがとうございました。／Thank you for going to all that trouble.
④ わざわざすみません。／Sorry to have made you go to all that trouble.

1. V ないでください。 ＜negative request (prohibition)＞
“V ないでください” is the negative form of the request pattern “V てください”, and is mostly
used to express prohibition. It can be translated as “please don't ...”, “do not ...”, etc.
① ここではタバコを吸わないでください。／Please do not smoke here.
② 危ないですから、椅子に登らないでください。／It's dangerous, so please don't climb on the
chair.
③ 写真を撮らないでください。／Please do not take photos.
2. V てもいい ＜permission＞
A verb followed by “てもいい” expresses permission for (the other party) to do something, equivalent to “you may
....” When “V てもいい” is used as a question, the subject is usually the first person (“わたし”) — the speaker
themselves — and is often omitted, equivalent to “may I ...?” Also, the “いい” in the pattern “V
てもいい” can sometimes be replaced with “大丈夫”.
① A：この本を借りてもいいですか。／May I borrow this book?
② 来 週 のパーティーに彼女を連れてきてもいいですよ。／You may bring your girlfriend to next week's
party.
③ A：こちらの資 料 を印刷しても大 丈 夫ですか。／May I print this mate-
rial?
B：はい、大丈夫ですよ。／Yes, that's fine.
The verb nai-form followed by “なくてもいい” expresses permitting someone not to do something, translatable as “you don't
have to ...”, “it's all right not to ....”
① 返さなくてもいいです。／You don't have to return it.
② 重い本は明日、持ってこなくてもいいですよ。／You don't have to bring the heavy books
tomorrow.
③ 急ぎませんので、今日は決めなくてもいいですよ。／There's no rush, so you don't have to decide
today.
A verb followed by “てはいけない” expresses prohibition, translatable as “must not ...”, “you are not allowed to
...”. It is mostly used for requirements from superiors to subordinates, or to state rules and discipline.
(must not) play outside until late.
② 図書館では飲み物を机の上に置いてはいけません。／In the library, you must not
leave drinks on the desk.
③ 食べ物を図書館に持ち込んではいけません。／Food must not be brought into the library.
5. V なければならない ＜have to; obligation＞
The verb nai-form followed by “なければならない” means “must”, “have to”. It expresses
the necessity or obligation to do an action. Patterns with similar meanings to “V なければならない” include:
“V なくてはいけない”, “V なければいけない”, and “V なくてはな
らない”. In spoken language, “V なければ” can be shortened to “V なきゃ”, and “V なくては” can be short-
ened to “V なくちゃ”.
① 日本人の家に入る時、靴を脱がなければなりません。／When entering a Japanese
person's home, you must take off your shoes.
In Japan, seatbelts must be fastened even in the back seat of a car.
③ せっかくの休みですが、仕事が終わらないので、残業しなければなら
ないんです。／It's a rare day off, but because the work isn't finished,
I have to work overtime.
6. V ることができる ＜able to＞
The verb dictionary form followed by “ことができる” expresses “being able to (do something).” Here,
“able” can mean either the ability to do something or having the conditions to do it, translatable as
“can ...”, “be able to ....” For example:
① ドイツ語を話すことができますか。／Can you speak German?
Now that the report is written, I can report to everyone tomorrow.
③ おかげさまで、無事に退院することができました。／Thanks to you, I was able to
leave the hospital safely.
7. N だけ + particle ＜limitation＞
“だけ” can attach to a noun to express limitation, translatable as “only”, “just”, etc. Depending on the
needs of the sentence, “だけ” can be followed by particles like “で”, “に”, “は”, “を”, “が”; when followed by “を” or
“が”, those particles can be omitted.

③ お金がないので、今日のお昼ご飯はサンドイッチだけで済ませます。
／Since I have no money, I'll make do with just a sandwich for lunch today.
In this lesson, “けっこうです” means “that's fine”, expressing approval by someone with the authority
to decide of another person's words or actions. Note that when expressing approval, “けっこうです”
cannot be used toward someone of higher status.
“けっこうです” can also be used to decline someone, translatable as “no thank you; I've had enough.”
When expressing refusal, “けっこうです” is a fairly polite expression and can also be used toward someone of higher sta-
tus. Which meaning “けっこうです” has must be judged from the context and the speaker's
tone. For example:
① A：紅茶をもう少しいかがですか。／Would you like some more tea?
B：もうけっこうです。／No, thank you (I've had enough).
② A：明日は来なくてもいいですか。／Is it all right if I don't come tomorrow?
③ せっかくのお誘いですが、わたしはけっこうです。／I appreciate the kind
invitation, but I'll pass this time.

A noun, or the dictionary form of a verb or adjective, followed by “とともに” expresses the coexistence of two

Pattern: V ます + つつある
The verb masu-stem followed by “つつある” expresses an ongoing change of state, translatable as “be ...ing (gradually).”

Pattern: V ない + んばかり
The verb nai-form (V ない) followed by “んばかり” (when “する” is followed by “んばかり”, it be-
comes “せんばかり”) expresses that a scene or state is on the verge of reaching the degree of the preceding verb,
equivalent to “今にも～しそうなくらい～”; translatable as “as if about to ...”,
“on the verge of ...”. Note that the former part expresses the degree of an action — the action was not actually carried out.
“〜んばかり” can appear mid-sentence, at the end of a sentence, or modifying another noun. In addition, it often appears in the form “～
と言わんばかり”, expressing that although it was not actually said out loud, the attitude gives that impression.
